tamil:
சுடச்சுடரும் பொன்போல் ஒளிவிடும் துன்பஞ்
சுடச்சுட நோற்கிற் பவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Sudachchudarum ponpol olividum thunbanj
Sudachchuda notkirpavarkku.
current_meaning: Gold shines brighter the more it is heated in fire. In the same way, people who practice self-control shine brighter the more suffering burns them.
elementary: When gold is put in a very hot fire, the dirt burns away and it becomes shinier. Valluvar says hard times do the same for a patient, disciplined person: every difficulty makes them shine brighter.
university: Among the most celebrated images in the Kural, the verse exploits the reduplicated சுடச்சுட (‘as it burns and burns’) twice — once for the goldsmith’s crucible and once for suffering — binding metaphor and meaning through sound. The figure also restores the etymological heart of tapas, from the Sanskrit root tap, ‘to heat, burn’, a notion also present in the Tamil நோன்பு/நோற்றல் of endurance. Commentators differ on what ‘shines’: Varadarasan and Pappaiah say true knowledge (மெய்யுணர்வு, ஞானம்), Kalaignar says reputation. The refining-fire metaphor is one of the most widely shared images in world religious literature, making this verse unusually rich in parallels.

tamil:
தன்னுயிர் தான்அறப் பெற்றானை ஏனைய
மன்னுயி ரெல்லாந் தொழும்.
transliteration:
Thannuyir thaan arap petraanai enaiya
Mannuyir ellaam thozhum.
current_meaning: A person who has fully let go of thinking about “me” and “my life” is honored by every other living being in the world.
elementary: Most of us think ‘me first’. A person who, after lots of practice, stops thinking ‘me, me, me’ becomes so good and gentle that everyone — people and even animals — looks up to them.
university: The first line is famously compressed: தன்னுயிர் தான் அறப் பெற்றான் can be read as ‘one who has become rid of [attachment to] his own life and of the ego “I”’ (Parimelazhagar, Varadarasan) or as ‘one who has fully gained possession of his own self’ (Pope’s ‘utter self-control’). Both readings converge on self-mastery culminating in egolessness. The consequence — ‘all other enduring lives worship him’ — echoes the Indian belief, also found in Jain and yogic texts, that the ahiṃsā-perfected sage commands the reverence even of animals. Placed after 267, the verse presents egolessness as the gold that emerges from the refining fire.

tamil:
கூற்றம் குதித்தலும் கைகூடும் நோற்றலின்
ஆற்றல் தலைப்பட் டவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Kootram kudhiththalum kaikoodum notralin
Aatral thalaippattavarkku.
current_meaning: For people who have gained the power that comes from strict self-control, even getting past death itself becomes possible.
elementary: Everyone is scared of death, like a giant monster nobody can beat. Valluvar says a person who has become really strong through tapas can even jump right over that monster.
university: கூற்றம் (Kūṟṟam), ‘the one who separates [soul from body]’, is the Tamil personification of Death, identified with Yama; குதித்தல் means to leap over or escape. The inclusive உம் (‘even’) signals this as the ultimate limit case of tapas-power, following the curse-and-blessing powers of 264. The medieval commentator Manakkudavar explicitly glosses the verse with the legend of Markandeya, the boy-devotee who escaped Yama’s noose, while Parimelazhagar identifies ஆற்றல் as the power of curse and grace. Philosophically, the verse can also be read as conquest of the fear of death, or as liberation from the cycle of births — interpretations that let the verse speak beyond its mythological frame.

tamil:
இலர்பல ராகிய காரணம் நோற்பார்
சிலர்பலர் நோலா தவர்.
transliteration:
Ilar palar aagiya kaaranam norpaar
Silar palar nolaadhavar.
current_meaning: So many people in the world have nothing because only a few practice strict self-control, and most do not.
elementary: In a class, only a few kids practise every day, and most don’t. That is why only a few become really good. Valluvar says the same about the whole world: most people are ‘poor’ inside because only a few do the hard work of tapas.
university: The closing couplet uses a neat chiastic arithmetic — இலர் பலர் (the have-nots are many) because நோற்பார் சிலர், பலர் நோலாதவர் (the practisers are few, the non-practisers many). இலர் is ambiguous: Solomon Pappaiah reads material poverty, Varadarasan and Kalaignar read lack of strength, and Puliyur Kesikan reads lack of true knowledge. The choice matters: a literal economic reading makes tapas a cause of prosperity, while the spiritual reading makes it the cause of inner wealth. Either way the verse ends the chapter with a sober sociology of virtue — excellence is rare because discipline is rare — and turns the whole chapter into an exhortation to join the few.

tamil:
வஞ்ச மனத்தான் படிற்றொழுக்கம் பூதங்கள்
ஐந்தும் அகத்தே நகும்.
transliteration:
Vanja manaththaan padittrozhukkam boodhangal
Aindhum agaththe nagum.
current_meaning: When someone with a lying mind pretends to live a holy life, the five elements that make up their own body laugh at them from inside.
elementary: Imagine someone pretending to be very good while secretly cheating. People outside might be fooled, but the earth, water, fire, air and sky that his body is made of can see everything — and they giggle at the silly act. You can’t hide a lie from the stuff you are made of.
university: The chapter opens with a striking image: the five great elements (pancha bhutas — earth, water, fire, air, ether) that compose the hypocrite’s body are themselves the witnesses who see through his sham piety and laugh inwardly. The word படிற்றொழுக்கம் (padittrozhukkam) denotes counterfeit or disguised conduct, and அகத்தே (agaththe) plays on “inside” — both inside the body and inside themselves. The point is that concealment is metaphysically impossible: the deceiver carries his witnesses with him. Parimelazhagar’s tradition reads the elements’ laughter as mockery of a man who thinks he can fool the world while his own substance knows the truth — a theme paralleled by Manu’s list of cosmic witnesses and the Qur’anic image of skins testifying.

tamil:
வானுயர் தோற்றம் எவன்செய்யும் தன்னெஞ்சம்
தான்அறி குற்றப் படின்.
transliteration:
Vaanuyar thotram evanseyyum thannenjam
Thaanari kutrap padin.
current_meaning: What good is looking as holy as the sky is high, if your own heart is full of wrongs that you yourself know about?
elementary: Suppose you wear a shiny superhero costume, but inside you know you just took your friend’s toy without asking. The costume doesn’t make you a hero. What you know about yourself matters more than how you look.
university: வானுயர் தோற்றம் (“a sky-high appearance”) refers to the imposing garb and bearing of the ascetic, and Valluvar poses a rhetorical question: of what use is it? The criterion he sets is not public exposure but self-knowledge — தன்னெஞ்சம் தான் அறி குற்றம், the fault the heart itself is aware of. Valluvar thus locates moral judgement in conscience rather than reputation, a remarkably interior standard for an ancient ethical text. The kural parallels the Gita’s notion of mithyācāra (the pretender whose mind dwells on what his outward restraint pretends to renounce), and Stoic ideas of conscience as the one witness who cannot be deceived.

tamil:
வலியில் நிலைமையான் வல்லுருவம் பெற்றம்
புலியின்தோல் போர்த்துமேய்ந் தற்று.
transliteration:
Valiyil nilaimaiyaan valluruvam petram
Puliyinthol porththumeindh thatru.
current_meaning: Someone with no control over themselves who dresses up like a strict holy person is like a cow eating crops while wearing a tiger's skin.
elementary: Picture a cow wearing a tiger costume so it can sneak into a farm and eat the crops. It looks scary, but it’s still just a cow munching grass. A person who dresses like a strong holy person but can’t control himself is the same — a costume on the outside, the same old habits inside.
university: The simile is doubly pointed: the cow is weak, not fierce, and the tiger-skin lends it a borrowed terror that lets it graze unchallenged on another’s field. வலியில் நிலைமையான் (“one lacking the strength” — traditionally, strength to restrain the senses) contrasts with வல்லுருவம் (“a mighty form”), the forbidding garb of tapas. The target is not ordinary weakness but the exploitation of a sacred appearance to feed appetite. The same fable circulated widely in the ancient world — the Panchatantra’s ass in the tiger-skin and Aesop’s ass in the lion’s skin — and in both the disguise ultimately betrays itself.

tamil:
தவமறைந்து அல்லவை செய்தல் புதல்மறைந்து
வேட்டுவன் புள்சிமிழ்த் தற்று.
transliteration:
Thavamaraindhu allavai seydhal pudhalmaraindhu
Vettuvan pulsimizhth thatru.
current_meaning: Hiding behind a holy look while doing wrong is like a hunter hiding behind a bush to trap birds.
elementary: A bird hunter hides in a bush so the birds think it’s just a plant, and then — snap! — he catches them. Someone who pretends to be holy so people trust him, and then tricks them, is doing the same thing. The holy look is just his hiding bush.
university: Valluvar here turns from the hypocrite’s inner weakness to his active predation. The verb மறைந்து (“hiding”) appears twice in parallel — தவம் மறைந்து / புதல் மறைந்து — making tapas itself the thicket, the camouflage that renders the trapper invisible to his prey. The trusting public are the birds (புள்), drawn close precisely because the cover looks harmless and natural. This anticipates the widespread Indian motif of the “cat-ascetic” (baiḍāla-vratika) who adopts vows to lure victims — condemned in both the Mahabharata and Manu — and resonates with Jesus’ charge that the Pharisees ‘for a pretence make long prayer’ while devouring widows’ houses.

tamil:
பற்றற்றேம் என்பார் படிற்றொழுக்கம் எற்றெற்றென்று
ஏதம் பலவுந் தரும்.
transliteration:
Patratrem enbaar padittrozhukkam etretrendru
Edham palavum tharum.
current_meaning: People who say, “We have given up all wanting,” but live falsely will face many troubles that make them cry, “What have we done! What have we done!”
elementary: If you tell everyone you gave up sweets, but secretly eat them all, one day you’ll be caught — and you’ll feel terrible and say, “Why did I do that?” Pretending costs more in the end than being honest.
university: The kural records the hypocrite’s own claim — பற்றற்றேம் (“we are free of attachment”) — and sets against it his eventual cry, எற்று எற்று (“what [have we done], what!”), an onomatopoeic doubled lament unusual in the Kural. Valluvar’s focus is on consequences: படிற்றொழுக்கம் (disguised conduct) produces ஏதம் பலவும், “many evils,” culminating in bitter self-reproach. The phrase may refer both to worldly ruin when the imposture is exposed and to karmic suffering afterwards. The pattern — pretended renunciation leading to anguished regret — is echoed in Manu’s consignment of ‘cat’ and ‘heron’ ascetics to hell and in Jesus’ ‘weeping and gnashing of teeth’ for hypocrites.

tamil:
நெஞ்சின் துறவார் துறந்தார்போல் வஞ்சித்து
வாழ்வாரின் வன்கணார் இல்.
transliteration:
Nenjin thuravaar thurandhaarpol vanjiththu
Vaazhvaarin vankanaar il.
current_meaning: No one is more hard-hearted than people who have not truly given up the world in their hearts, yet trick others by acting as if they have.
elementary: Some people pretend to be kind helpers who need nothing, so others trust them and give them things — but secretly they are greedy. Valluvar says that tricking people who trust you like this is about the meanest thing a person can do.
university: Valluvar’s strongest verdict in the chapter uses வன்கணார் — literally “the hard-eyed,” those without compassion — and makes it superlative: none are worse (இல்). The contrast நெஞ்சின் துறவார் / துறந்தார்போல் (“not renounced in heart” / “like those who renounced”) sharpens the gap between inner reality and outward role. The special cruelty lies in exploiting the reverence and generosity that society extends to genuine renunciants, and so corrupting the very institution of trust. Plato made the same ranking when Adeimantus and Glaucon called seeming-just-while-being-unjust the ‘highest reach’ of injustice, and Manu classes such pretenders as ‘cats’ bent on doing injury.

tamil:
புறங்குன்றி கண்டனைய ரேனும் அகங்குன்றி
முக்கிற் கரியார் உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Purangundri kandanaiya renum agangundri
Mukkir kariyaar udaiththu.
current_meaning: Some people are bright red on the outside like the kundri seed (a small red seed), but inside they are as black as the seed's dark tip.
elementary: There’s a tiny seed that is shiny red all over — except for one small black spot. Some people are like that: they look bright and good on the outside, but they hide a dark spot inside. Don’t judge only by the shiny part.
university: The kundri (குன்றி, Abrus precatorius) is a brilliant scarlet seed with a black spot at its ‘nose’ (மூக்கு); Valluvar makes it an emblem of the hypocrite, crimson-bright in outward piety, black at the core. The line plays on the repeated குன்றி in புறம் (outer) and அகம் (inner) — the fundamental Tamil poetic pair — so that the seed embodies both states at once. The seed was also used as a jeweller’s weight and is poisonous, which adds a latent irony: something small, attractive and valued conceals toxicity. The image anticipates Jesus’ ‘whited sepulchres’ and Hesiod’s Pandora — beauty outside, deceit within.

tamil:
மனத்தது மாசாக மாண்டார் நீராடி
மறைந்தொழுகு மாந்தர் பலர்.
transliteration:
Manaththadhu maasaaga maandaar neeraadi
Maraindhozhugu maandhar palar.
current_meaning: Many people with dirty minds bathe in holy waters as if they were great people, and they hide behind that show.
elementary: Taking a bath gets the dirt off your skin — but it can’t wash away a mean or dishonest thought. Some people make a big show of holy bathing so everyone thinks they’re pure, but inside they’re still dirty. Clean hands don’t mean a clean heart.
university: Ritual bathing (நீராடல்) was the most visible sign of purity in both Brahmanical and Tamil religious life; Valluvar turns it into an instrument of concealment. The phrase மாண்டார் நீராடி can be read ‘bathing like the great (மாண்டார்)’ — imitating the ablutions of true sages — and மறைந்தொழுகு (‘conduct in hiding’) suggests that the water itself becomes a screen, as Kalaignar’s gloss has it: submerged, the bather disappears. The mind (மனம்) is the site of மாசு (impurity), echoing Kural 34’s definition of dharma as a mind free of stain. Across traditions, from Isaiah’s ‘Wash you, make you clean’ to Heraclitus mocking blood-purification, the same protest is made: outward ablution cannot cleanse inward defilement.

tamil:
கணைகொடிது யாழ்கோடு செவ்விதுஆங் கன்ன
வினைபடு பாலால் கொளல்.
transliteration:
Kanaikodidhu yaazhkodu sevvidhuaang kanna
Vinaipadu paalaal kolal.
current_meaning: An arrow is straight but does harm. A lute (a stringed instrument) is bent but makes sweet music. So judge people by what they do, not by how they look.
elementary: An arrow looks perfectly straight, but it’s made for hurting. A guitar has a curvy neck, but it makes lovely music. So don’t decide who is good just by how they look — watch what they actually do.
university: Here Valluvar moves from condemnation to method: how can one tell the hypocrite from the saint? The paired images turn the usual metaphors upside down — கணை (arrow) is straight yet கொடிது (cruel), while யாழ்கோடு (the curved neck of the yazh, the ancient Tamil harp-lute) is bent yet செவ்விது (upright, good). Since செம்மை and கொடுமை mean both ‘straight/crooked’ and ‘good/cruel’, the kural exploits the double meaning to show that visual straightness and moral straightness are different things. The conclusion — வினைபடு பாலால் கொளல், ‘assess by the quality of deeds’ — is a pragmatic epistemology of character that parallels Jesus’ ‘by their fruits ye shall know them’ and the Yaksha’s answer that conduct, not birth or learning, makes a Brahmin.

tamil:
மழித்தலும் நீட்டலும் வேண்டா உலகம்
பழித்தது ஒழித்து விடின்.
transliteration:
Mazhiththalum neettalum vendaa ulagam
Pazhiththadhu ozhiththu vidin.
current_meaning: There is no need to shave your head or to grow your hair long, if you simply give up what the world says is wrong.
elementary: Some holy people shave their heads and some grow their hair really long. Valluvar says: your haircut doesn’t make you good! If you stop doing bad things, you’re already on the right path — hair or no hair.
university: The chapter closes with its most famous and most radical line. மழித்தல் (shaving the head, as Jain and Buddhist monks did) and நீட்டல் (growing matted locks, as Shaiva and Vedic ascetics did) were the defining visual signs of rival renunciant orders; Valluvar dismisses both in a single breath, declaring them unnecessary (வேண்டா). The only real requirement is ethical: உலகம் பழித்தது ஒழித்தல் — abandoning what the wise of the world condemn. This non-sectarian move, placing conduct above every order’s insignia, is characteristic of the Kural as a whole and parallels the Dhammapada’s dismissal of tonsure and matted hair, Manu’s ‘the external mark is not the cause of merit’, and Seneca’s warning against the philosopher’s unkempt beard.

tamil:
எள்ளாமை வேண்டுவான் என்பான் எனைத்தொன்றும்
கள்ளாமை காக்கதன் நெஞ்சு.
transliteration:
Ellaamai venduvaan enbaan enaiththondrum,
Kallaamai kaakkathan nenju.
current_meaning: If you never want to be looked down on, guard your heart so it never even plans to steal anything at all from anyone, even something small.
elementary: Nobody wants to be laughed at or called a cheat. The way to make sure that never happens is to keep a guard at the door of your own mind, so that even the idea of sneaking away something that isn’t yours — even a pencil — never gets in.
university: The chapter opens by locating fraud (kaḷavu) not in the hand but in the heart (neñcu): the verb is kākka, “let him guard,” and its object is the mind itself. Valluvar’s motive clause is social and reputational — eḷḷāmai, “not being scorned” — which fits the householder-and-ascetic audience of the Tuṟavaṟaviyal section, where public trust is the currency of a moral life. The word eṉaittoṉṟum (“anything whatsoever”) forecloses the familiar rationalisation that small frauds do not count, anticipating the Aristotelian claim that theft admits no virtuous mean. Commentators from Parimēlaḻakar to Mu. Varadarasan read kaḷḷāmai as covering not only burglary but every covert appropriation, including short-changing and deceit in dealings.

tamil:
உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளலும் தீதே பிறன்பொருளைக்
கள்ளத்தால் கள்வேம் எனல்.
transliteration:
Ullaththaal ullalum theethe piranporulaik,
Kallaththaal kalvem enal.
current_meaning: Even thinking in your mind, “I will trick them and take what they own,” is wrong.
elementary: Imagine thinking, “When no one is looking, I’ll trick my friend out of his toy.” Even if you never do it, just planning it is already a bad step, because every wrong action begins as a thought.
university: Valluvar moves culpability upstream from act to intention: uḷḷattāl uḷḷalum tītē — “even the thinking with the mind is evil.” The phrase kaḷḷattāl kaḷvēm (“we shall steal by craft”) specifies the content of the forbidden thought as a deliberate scheme, not a passing temptation, which is important for the ethical claim. This parallels the Tenth Commandment’s ban on coveting, the Buddhist teaching that mind precedes action, and the Gita’s account of how dwelling on objects breeds desire. Commentators note the psychological realism: fraud requires premeditation, so the only reliable defence is to refuse the premeditation itself.

tamil:
களவினால் ஆகிய ஆக்கம் அளவிறந்து
ஆவது போலக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Kalavinaal aakiya aakkam alavirandhu,
Aavadhu polak kedum.
current_meaning: Riches gained by cheating may seem to grow beyond measure, but they will be lost, and they will take more with them than they brought.
elementary: It’s like a soap bubble: a stolen treasure puffs up bigger and bigger and looks amazing, and then — pop! — it’s gone, and it can even splash away the things you already had.
university: The couplet turns on the paradox of āvatu pōla, “as if growing”: fraudulent gain has the appearance of prosperity but not its substance. The phrase aḷaviṟantu is read two ways by commentators — as “beyond measure” describing the apparent growth, or (with Mu. Varadarasan and Kalaignar) as the ruin exceeding its natural limit and consuming even legitimately held wealth. Either way, Valluvar denies the fraudster even a prudential victory. The same instability of ill-gotten wealth is a commonplace across Hesiod, Proverbs, Jeremiah and the Qur’an, suggesting a widely shared moral-economic intuition that dishonest gain lacks durable foundations.

tamil:
களவின்கண் கன்றிய காதல் விளைவின்கண்
வீயா விழுமம் தரும்.
transliteration:
Kalavinkan kandriya kaadhal vilaivinkan,
Veeyaa vizhumam tharum.
current_meaning: A deep habit of wanting to gain by cheating will, when it finally bears fruit, bring sorrow that never ends.
elementary: Wanting to cheat is like planting a thorn bush because its flowers look pretty. When it grows up, the thorns keep poking you, and you can never get rid of them.
university: Kaṉṟiya kātal — a desire that has become hardened or habitual — is the subject, and the agricultural verb viḷaivu (ripening, harvest) sets up the karmic metaphor: fraud is a seed whose fruit is vīyā viḻumam, “unperishing affliction.” The emphasis on habit links this couplet to 286 and 288, where Valluvar treats fraud as a character formed by repetition. The imagery of delayed but certain ripening is close to the Dhammapada’s description of evil deeds that seem sweet until they ripen. Commentators split between reading the sorrow as this-worldly (disgrace, punishment) and as extending into later births; the adjective vīyā allows both.

tamil:
அருள்கருதி அன்புடைய ராதல் பொருள்கருதிப்
பொச்சாப்புப் பார்ப்பார்கண் இல்.
transliteration:
Arulkarudhi anbudaiya raadhal porulkarudhip,
Pochchaappup paarppaarkan il.
current_meaning: People who want others' things and wait for the moment someone is not paying attention cannot be loving people who care about kindness.
elementary: A real friend helps you when you drop your lunch money. Someone who waits for you to drop it so they can grab it can’t be kind at the same time — the waiting-to-grab heart pushes the kindness out.
university: The couplet contrasts two inner orientations: aruḷ karuti, “holding grace (compassion) in regard,” and poruḷ karuti, “holding another’s wealth in regard.” The fraudster’s signature act is poccāppu pārttal — watching for the other person’s forgetfulness or unguardedness — which Valluvar treats as incompatible with aṉpu (love). The couplet ties this chapter to the preceding ones on Aruḷuṭaimai (compassion), showing that for Valluvar honesty in dealings is not a separate commercial rule but a consequence of compassion. Kant’s shopkeeper, the hadith of the wet grain, and Micah’s schemers lying awake all describe the same failure: treating another person’s vulnerability as an opportunity.

tamil:
அளவின்கண் நின்றொழுகல் ஆற்றார் களவின்கண்
கன்றிய காத லவர்.
transliteration:
Alavinkan nindrozhugal aatraar kalavinkan,
Kandriya kaadha lavar.
current_meaning: People with a hardened love for gaining by cheating cannot keep their actions within proper limits.
elementary: A scale in a shop is supposed to measure fairly. Someone who loves cheating is like a scale with a broken spring — it can’t stay steady, and it keeps tipping the wrong way.
university: Aḷavu (“measure, limit”) is the key term of the second half of the chapter (286-289), and Valluvar plays on its near-rhyme with kaḷavu (“fraud, theft”). Commentators differ on what aḷavu means: Parimēlaḻakar takes it as the ascetic’s limited livelihood, Mu. Varadarasan as thrift or contentment, others as the rule of right conduct. The rhyme itself makes the point that fraud is a failure of measure, which is why honest weights and measures are the concrete test in Leviticus, Deuteronomy, the Qur’an and the Buddhist suttas. The couplet repeats kaṉṟiya kātal from 284, presenting fraud as a habit that eats away the ability to keep within limits.

tamil:
களவென்னும் காரறி வாண்மை அளவென்னும்
ஆற்றல் புரிந்தார்கண் இல்.
transliteration:
Kalavennum kaarari vaanmai alavennum,
Aatral purindhaarkan il.
current_meaning: The dark cleverness called cheating is not found in those who have chosen the strength of knowing their limits.
elementary: Some people are clever in a sneaky, shadowy way. But a person who has learned to be happy with a fair share has a brighter kind of strength, and the sneaky cleverness simply has no room to live in them.
university: Kār aṟivu — literally “black knowledge” — is Valluvar’s striking name for fraud: an intelligence that is real but darkened, directed at deception rather than understanding. He opposes to it aḷavu eṉṉum āṟṟal, “the power called measure,” so that restraint is framed not as weakness but as a form of strength. The contrast anticipates Aristotle’s distinction between practical wisdom and mere cleverness (deinotēs), which can serve bad ends. Textual note: some online editions print the last word-group as புரிந்தார்கண்ட இல்; the reading புரிந்தார்கண் இல் given here follows Tamil Surangam and thirukkural-thamizh.org and fits the metre.

tamil:
அளவறிந்தார் நெஞ்சத் தறம்போல நிற்கும்
களவறிந்தார் நெஞ்சில் கரவு.
transliteration:
Alavarindhaar nenjath tharampola nirkum,
Kalavarindhaar nenjil karavu.
current_meaning: Goodness stays firmly in the hearts of people who know their limits. In the same way, trickery stays firmly in the hearts of people who have learned to cheat.
elementary: Your heart is like a room. If you practise being fair, fairness moves in and makes itself at home. If you practise cheating, sneakiness moves in instead — and whoever lives there decides how you act.
university: The couplet is built on precise parallelism — aḷavu aṟintār / kaḷavu aṟintār (“those who know measure / those who know fraud”) — with the verb niṟkum (“stands, abides”) serving both halves. The point is that virtue and deceit (karavu, “concealment”) are both settled dispositions formed by what one has come to “know” through practice. This is close to Aristotle’s claim that we become just or unjust through our dealings with others, and to the Gospel image of the heart as a treasury from which good or evil is brought out. It also explains 284 and 286: once fraud is ‘known’ in this habitual sense, concealment becomes the heart’s standing condition.

tamil:
அளவல்ல செய்தாங்கே வீவர் களவல்ல
மற்றைய தேற்றா தவர்.
transliteration:
Alavalla seydhaange veevar kalavalla,
Matraiya thetraa thavar.
current_meaning: People who know no way to live except cheating will be destroyed right in the middle of their wrong deeds.
elementary: If the only trick you know is cheating, it’s like a player who only knows how to foul — sooner or later, right in the middle of the game, they get caught and sent off.
university: The couplet says the fraudster’s ruin is not deferred but comes āṅkē — “right there,” in the act itself. The phrase kaḷavu alla maṟṟaiya tēṟṟātavar (“those who do not understand anything other than fraud”) describes a person whose repertoire has narrowed to one method, which completes the habituation argument of 288. Plato gives a striking parallel: a completely unjust person could not act at all, because cooperation depends on some remnant of justice. Acts 5’s account of Ananias, struck down while misrepresenting a sale, is the most literal illustration of perishing ‘right there.’

tamil:
கள்வார்க்குத் தள்ளும் உயிர்நிலை கள்ளார்க்குத்
தள்ளாது புத்தேள் உலகு.
transliteration:
Kalvaarkkuth thallum uyirnilai kallaarkkuth,
Thallaadhu puththel ulagu.
current_meaning: For people who cheat, even their own life in the body will fail them. For people who never cheat, even the world of the gods will not fail them.
elementary: Cheaters can lose even the simple things everyone needs, like a safe life. People who stay honest are promised the biggest prize of all, like a door to heaven that will always open for them.
university: The chapter ends with an antithesis built on one verb, taḷḷu (“to fail, to reject”): life itself (uyirnilai, the soul’s stay in the body) ‘fails’ the kaḷvār, while the world of the gods (puttēḷ ulaku) ‘does not fail’ the kaḷḷār. Solomon Pappaiah reads the first clause vividly as ‘even their own life shuns the thief.’ Textual note: some online editions repeat கள்வார்க்குத் in the second line, but the antithesis requires கள்ளார்க்குத் (“to those who do not defraud”), which is the reading of Tamil Surangam, thirukkural-thamizh.org and the standard commentaries. The contrast of this-worldly collapse with heavenly reward parallels 1 Corinthians 6:10, the Chandogya Upanishad’s list of those who ‘fall,’ and the Talmud’s first question at the heavenly court.

tamil:
வாய்மை எனப்படுவது யாதெனின் யாதொன்றும்
தீமை இலாத சொலல்.
transliteration:
Vaaymai enappaduvadhu yaadhenin yaadhondrum
Theemai ilaadha solal.
current_meaning: If you ask what truthfulness is, it is speaking words that cause no harm of any kind to anyone.
elementary: Being truthful isn’t only about not telling lies. Imagine your words are like gifts you hand to people — a truthful gift is one that never hurts anybody. So truth means saying things that are real AND that don’t cause harm.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter with a deliberately surprising definition: vaaymai is not defined by correspondence to fact (the usual Western criterion) but by its effect — speech ‘without even the least evil’ (yaadhondrum theemai ilaadha). The standard commentators (Parimelazhagar, Mu. Varadarasan, Solomon Pappaiah) all read theemai as harm to others, so truth becomes an ethical rather than merely epistemic category. This places the Kural within the broader Indian tradition that fuses satya with ahimsa, and it sets up the controversial next couplet (292) on beneficial untruth. The verse’s rhetorical form — a question answered in a definition (enappaduvadhu yaadhenin, ‘if one asks what is called…’) — marks it as the chapter’s thesis statement.

tamil:
பொய்மையும் வாய்மை யிடத்த புரைதீர்ந்த
நன்மை பயக்கும் எனின்.
transliteration:
Poymaiyum vaaymai yidaththa puraitheerndha
Nanmai payakkum enin.
current_meaning: Even a lie can count as the truth if it brings about pure good with no harm in it.
elementary: Imagine a friend is scared before a big test and asks if they look nervous. Saying “You look calm and ready!” — to help them, not to trick them for your own gain — is the kind of “kind untruth” this kural talks about. But it only counts if it does real good and hurts no one.
university: This is one of the most debated couplets in the Kural. Having defined truth by harmlessness in 291, Valluvar draws the logical consequence: a statement that is factually false but yields ‘faultless good’ (puraitheerndha nanmai) occupies ‘the place of truth’ (vaaymai idaththa). The qualifier purai theerndha — ‘with the defect removed’ — is strict: the good must be free of any taint, not merely useful to the speaker. Commentators diverge on scope: Varadarasan says such words ‘obtain the place’ of truth; Pappaiah reads it as permission to speak falsely where truth would otherwise be required. The verse places the Kural in a consequentialist line of Indian ethics (compare Krishna’s teaching in the Mahabharata) rather than the absolutism of Kant or of Buddhist precept.

tamil:
தன்நெஞ் சறிவது பொய்யற்க பொய்த்தபின்
தன்நெஞ்சே தன்னைச் சுடும்.
transliteration:
Than nenju arivadhu poyyarka poyththapin
Than nenjae thannaich chudum.
current_meaning: Do not lie about what your own heart knows is true. Once you lie, your own heart will burn you with guilt.
elementary: Have you ever told a fib and then felt a hot, uncomfortable feeling inside, even if no one found out? That feeling is your own heart “burning” you. This kural says: don’t lie against what you know is true, because your conscience will punish you.
university: The couplet moves truthfulness from the social sphere into the interior. ‘Than nenju arivadhu’ — what one’s own heart knows — specifies a deliberate lie, one told against one’s own knowledge. The punishment is not external: ‘than nenjae thannaich chudum,’ the self’s own heart scorches the self. The repetition of than (self) three times across two lines enacts the reflexive structure of conscience. Kalaignar explicitly glosses nenju as manachaatchi, ‘conscience,’ and Pappaiah adds that the burning intensifies when the world discovers the lie — combining inner guilt with outer shame.

tamil:
உள்ளத்தாற் பொய்யா தொழுகின் உலகத்தார்
உள்ளத்து ளெல்லாம் உளன்.
transliteration:
Ullaththaal poyyaadhu ozhukin ulagaththaar
Ullaththul ellaam ulan.
current_meaning: A person who lives without lying, even inside their own heart, will have a place in the hearts of everyone in the world.
elementary: Think of someone you completely trust — a grandparent or a teacher who never tricks you. You carry them in your heart, don’t you? This kural says that if you are honest even inside your own thoughts, everyone will keep you in their hearts too.
university: The couplet is built on an elegant chiasmus of ullam (heart/mind): one who does not lie ‘with the heart’ (ullaththaal) comes to live ‘in the hearts’ (ullaththul) of all. Truthfulness here extends past speech to conduct (ozhukin, ‘if one conducts oneself’) and even to thought — Kalaignar reads it as not even thinking falsehood. The reward is not wealth or heaven but a permanent place in human regard, which links this chapter to the preceding chapter on fame (புகழ், ch. 24). Pappaiah narrows ‘ulagaththaar’ to the noble (uyarndhavar), following the classical reading of ulagam as ‘the worthy.’

tamil:
மனத்தொடு வாய்மை மொழியின் தவத்தொடு
தானஞ்செய் வாரின் தலை.
transliteration:
Manaththodu vaaymai mozhiyin thavaththodu
Thaanam seyvaarin thalai.
current_meaning: A person whose words are true and match their heart is greater than people who practice both strict self-control and giving to others.
elementary: Some people do hard things to look holy, like fasting, and some give lots of gifts. This kural says that someone who simply speaks the truth from the heart, every day, is even greater than people who do both of those big things.
university: Here Valluvar ranks truthfulness above the two most prestigious religious practices of his world: thavam (tapas, ascetic austerity, the subject of chapter 27) and dhaanam (charity/gift-giving). The qualifier manaththodu — ‘together with the mind’ — is decisive: only truth that agrees with inner conviction counts, not lip-truth (Kalaignar: ‘udhattalavil indri ulamaara,’ ‘not just from the lips but from the heart’). The couplet belongs to a broad pan-Indian and wider religious critique of ritualism, in which inner integrity outweighs outer observance. Its hierarchy — truth above tapas — is stated almost verbatim in the Mahabharata’s image of truth outweighing a hundred horse-sacrifices.

tamil:
பொய்யாமை அன்ன புகழில்லை எய்யாமை
எல்லா அறமுந் தரும்.
transliteration:
Poyyaamai anna pugazhillai eyyaamai
Ellaa aramum tharum.
current_meaning: No praise is as great as the praise for never lying. Without any extra effort, it brings every other good quality with it.
elementary: Being known as someone who never lies is the best reputation you can have. And it’s like a magnet — once you are truthful, other good habits, like fairness and kindness, come to you easily, without you even trying hard.
university: The couplet makes two claims: truthfulness is the supreme source of pugazh (fame, cf. ch. 24), and it ‘yields every dharma’ (ellaa aramum tharum). The pivot word eyyaamai is read in two ways: Parimelazhagar-line commentators take it as ‘without suffering/strain’ — truthfulness produces all virtue effortlessly, unlike painful austerity; Varadarasan and Pappaiah read it as ‘without one’s knowing it,’ i.e., the virtues accrue unnoticed. Either way the claim is that veracity is a generative, master virtue from which the others follow — a thesis close to the Islamic hadith that truthfulness leads to righteousness.

tamil:
பொய்யாமை பொய்யாமை ஆற்றின் அறம்பிற
செய்யாமை செய்யாமை நன்று.
transliteration:
Poyyaamai poyyaamai aatrin aram pira
Seyyaamai seyyaamai nandru.
current_meaning: If you are truthful and never fail at it, that is enough, even if you do no other good deed.
elementary: Imagine a report card where one subject counts so much that getting it right is enough to pass everything. For Valluvar, truthfulness is that subject: if you never fail at being honest, you’re doing well even if you haven’t done any other good deeds yet.
university: A celebrated example of Valluvar’s wordplay: poyyaamai poyyaamai (literally ‘non-lying, not failing’) and seyyaamai seyyaamai (‘not doing, not doing’). The first pair means practising non-falsehood unfailingly; the second is read by most commentators (Parimelazhagar, Pappaiah) as ‘not doing [other virtues] is itself not a lack’ — truth alone suffices. Varadarasan offers a softer reading (‘practising other virtues also becomes good’), and Kalaignar reads it as truthfulness surpassing the merit of mere abstentions. The dominant reading makes veracity a sufficient condition of the good life, the strongest claim in the chapter after 300.

tamil:
புறந்தூய்மை நீரான் அமையும் அகந்தூய்மை
வாய்மையால் காணப் படும்.
transliteration:
Purandhooymai neeraan amaiyum agandhooymai
Vaaymaiyaal kaanap padum.
current_meaning: Water makes a person clean on the outside. Being truthful shows that a person is clean on the inside.
elementary: When you get muddy, you take a bath and you’re clean on the outside. But how do you get clean on the inside? This kural says water can’t reach there — only telling the truth can wash your mind and heart.
university: The couplet sets up a clean binary: puram / agam (outer / inner), a pairing that also names the two great genres of classical Tamil poetry. Outer purity ‘is achieved’ (amaiyum) by water; inner purity ‘is seen / made manifest’ (kaanappadum) by truthfulness — truth both produces and reveals a clean mind. This is a pointed comment on ritual bathing (neeraadal) in holy waters. Textual note: several popular web editions print the first word as ‘புறள்தூய்மை’; the grammatically regular form ‘புறந்தூய்மை’ (puram + thooymai), used here, is attested in other editions and fits the parallel with அகந்தூய்மை.

tamil:
எல்லா விளக்கும் விளக்கல்ல சான்றோர்க்குப்
பொய்யா விளக்கே விளக்கு.
transliteration:
Ellaa vilakkum vilakkalla saandrorkkup
Poyyaa vilakke vilakku.
current_meaning: Not every lamp is a real lamp. For wise people, the lamp of truthfulness is the only real lamp.
elementary: A flashlight helps you see in a dark room. But what helps you see the right thing to do when you are confused inside? This kural says truthfulness is that special inner flashlight — and for wise people, it’s the only lamp that really matters.
university: The couplet repeats vilakku (lamp) four times, playing on its meanings: ordinary lamps dispel outer darkness, but ‘the lamp that does not lie’ (poyyaa vilakku) dispels inner darkness. Varadarasan’s gloss adds the parenthetical contrast explicitly: lamps that remove darkness outside versus the lamp of non-falsehood that removes darkness within. Saandror — the noble, the wise — is a key Kural term (cf. ch. 99, Saandraanmai), suggesting truthfulness is the defining light of the fully mature person. The truth-as-light metaphor is among the most widely shared images across religious traditions.

tamil:
யாமெய்யாக் கண்டவற்றுள் இல்லை எனைத்தொன்றும்
வாய்மையின் நல்ல பிற.
transliteration:
Yaam meyyaak kandavatrul illai enaiththondrum
Vaaymaiyin nalla pira.
current_meaning: Of all the things we have found to be truly real, there is nothing at all that is better than truthfulness.
elementary: Imagine you searched the whole world and all the best books for the most precious treasure. Valluvar says he did that kind of search — and the greatest treasure he found was simply telling the truth.
university: The chapter closes with a personal verdict — one of the rare places Valluvar speaks in the first person (yaam, ‘we’). ‘Meyyaak kandavai’ means ‘things seen/found as real,’ and there is a deliberate play between mey (reality, truth) and vaaymai (truthful speech): among all that is mey, nothing surpasses vaaymai. Pappaiah reads kandavai as ‘the books I have examined,’ making this a survey of all moral literature; Kalaignar takes it as the conclusion of research into what is true. Either way, the couplet sets veracity at the summit of all virtues, bringing the chapter full circle from its opening definition.

tamil:
செல்லிடத்துக் காப்பான் சினங்காப்பான் அல்லிடத்துக்
காக்கின்என் காவாக்கா லென்.
transliteration:
Sellidaththuk kaappaan sinangaappaan allidaththuk
Kaakkin en kaavaakkaal en.
current_meaning: Holding back anger only counts when you could actually hurt someone with it. If your anger has no power to do harm anyway, what does it matter whether you hold it back or not?
elementary: Imagine a big kid who could easily push a small kid, but chooses not to. That is real self-control. If a small kid can't push a big kid anyway, 'not pushing' isn't really a choice. This kural says being calm only counts when you really could have hurt someone and you don't.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter by redefining the virtue itself: restraint of anger (sinam kaaththal) is morally meaningful only where one has the power (sellidam, literally 'the place where it goes through') to make the anger effective. Classical commentators such as Parimelazhagar read sellidam as the case of anger toward those weaker than oneself, where retaliation would succeed; restraint toward the stronger is mere prudence or fear. The couplet thus locates virtue in the gap between capacity and action, anticipating the Aristotelian and Stoic view that a virtue is shown only where its opposite is genuinely available. The rhetorical question of the second line ('what if he guards it, what if he does not?') dismisses 'restraint' that costs nothing as morally empty.

tamil:
செல்லா இடத்துச் சினந்தீது செல்லிடத்தும்
இல்அதனின் தீய பிற.
transliteration:
Sellaa idaththuch sinandheedhu sellidaththum
Il adhanin theeya pira.
current_meaning: Getting angry at people stronger than you only hurts you. Getting angry at people weaker than you, who cannot fight back, is the worst evil of all.
elementary: If you get angry at a much bigger kid, you will probably get hurt. If you get angry at a much smaller kid, you might hurt them, and that is even worse. So anger is bad either way: it hurts you, or it makes you hurt someone who can't fight back.
university: This couplet completes the argument of 301 by closing every escape route: anger is bad where it is ineffective (sellaa idam, anger toward the powerful, which rebounds on oneself) and worst of all where it is effective (sellidam, anger toward the weak, which inflicts real injury). Mu. Varadarasanar's gloss makes the two cases explicit as 'stronger' and 'weaker' persons. The ethical weight falls on the second line: power over others magnifies the moral gravity of anger rather than licensing it. The structure anticipates modern concerns about abuse of authority in households, workplaces, and states, where anger combined with power becomes cruelty.

tamil:
மறத்தல் வெகுளியை யார்மாட்டும் தீய
பிறத்தல் அதனான் வரும்.
transliteration:
Maraththal vekuliyai yaarmaattum theeya
Piraththal adhanaan varum.
current_meaning: Let go of your anger at anyone at all, and forget it, because every kind of harm grows out of anger.
elementary: Anger is like a seed that grows weeds. If you keep it, bad things grow out of it: mean words, fights, broken friendships. So the kural says: let go of anger, no matter who made you angry.
university: The verb maraththal ('forgetting', 'letting go') is significant: Valluvar does not ask merely for suppression but for the anger to be dropped from memory, since resentment that is stored continues to generate harm. Yaarmaattum ('toward anyone whatsoever') universalises the precept, removing the distinctions of power drawn in 301 and 302. The second line offers a causal claim: evils (theeya) are 'born' (piraththal) from anger, making it a root vice rather than one fault among many. This genealogical view of anger as a source of other wrongs parallels the Buddhist treatment of dosa as one of the three roots of unwholesome action and the Gita's chain from desire to anger to ruin.

tamil:
நகையும் உவகையும் கொல்லும் சினத்தின்
பகையும் உளவோ பிற.
transliteration:
Nagaiyum uvagaiyum kollum sinaththin
Pagaiyum ulavo pira.
current_meaning: Anger kills the smile on your face and the joy in your heart. Is there any enemy worse than that?
elementary: When you are really angry, you can't laugh and you can't feel happy. It's like a thief that steals your smile. The kural asks: what enemy could be worse than one that takes away all your happiness?
university: Valluvar pairs nagai (laughter, the outward cheerfulness of the face) with uvagai (inner delight), a pairing the commentators render as 'face-blossoming and heart-blossoming'. Anger 'kills' both, so the damage is not only social but inward. The rhetorical question reframes anger as a pagai (enemy) that lives within, which is more dangerous than any external foe because it cannot be escaped. The idea of anger as an internal enemy runs through Indian thought (the 'six inner enemies', including krodha) and has close parallels in the Buddhist teaching that an angry person does to himself what an enemy would wish on him.

tamil:
தன்னைத்தான் காக்கின் சினங்காக்க காவாக்கால்
தன்னையே கொல்லுஞ் சினம்.
transliteration:
Thannaiththaan kaakkin sinangaakka kaavaakkaal
Thannaiye kollum sinam.
current_meaning: If you want to protect yourself, keep your anger in check. If you don’t, your own anger will destroy you.
elementary: Anger is like a fire you carry in your own pocket. If you don't put it out, it burns you first. So the best way to keep yourself safe is to keep anger away.
university: The couplet turns on the reflexive thannai ('oneself'), which frames it: the whole argument is about self-preservation, not the protection of others. Valluvar's point is strategic as much as moral: anger, left unguarded, turns back on its owner, destroying health, judgment, reputation, and eventually life. The repetition of kaa ('guard') across both lines makes guarding anger identical with guarding the self. This self-interested argument against anger complements the altruistic ones elsewhere in the chapter and matches Stoic and Buddhist analyses that anger harms its owner before its target.

tamil:
சினமென்னும் சேர்ந்தாரைக் கொல்லி இனமென்னும்
ஏமப் புணையைச் சுடும்.
transliteration:
Sinamennum serndhaaraik kolli inamennum
Emap punaiyaich sudum.
current_meaning: Anger is a fire that kills anyone who comes near it. It even burns up your family and friends, who are like a raft that carries you safely through life.
elementary: Think of your family and friends as a raft that keeps you floating in a big river. Anger is like a fire on that raft. If you let it burn, it destroys the very thing that keeps you safe.
university: The couplet is built on a compound metaphor. Sinam is called serndhaaraik kolli, 'the killer of those who come close', a traditional kenning for fire, which destroys whatever touches it. Inam, one's kin and circle of friends, is called an emap punai, a 'safe raft' that carries one across the dangerous sea of life. Anger, being fire, burns the very raft that was meant to save its owner: it isolates the angry person by consuming the relationships that sustain them. Valluvar thus extends the self-harm argument of 305 to its social dimension.

tamil:
சினத்தைப் பொருளென்று கொண்டவன் கேடு
நிலத்தறைந்தான் கைபிழையா தற்று.
transliteration:
Sinaththaip porulendru kondavan kedu
Nilaththaraindhaan kai pizhaiyaadhatru.
current_meaning: A person who treats anger as something precious will surely be ruined, just as someone who hits the ground with their hand will surely hurt that hand.
elementary: If you slap the floor as hard as you can, the floor doesn't feel anything, but your hand really hurts. Using anger as your 'power' is the same: the person who uses it gets hurt the most.
university: The target here is a specific attitude: treating anger as porul, a thing of worth or a useful tool, whether as a mark of strength, a way to command respect, or a means of getting results. The simile of striking the ground (nilaththu araindhaan) is precise: the ground is unharmed while the striker's hand is certain to be injured, so anger's force rebounds on its user. Kai pizhaiyaadhu ('the hand does not escape') stresses certainty, not mere probability. The couplet enters a long-running debate, found in Aristotle and Seneca, about whether anger is a useful servant of virtue; Valluvar sides firmly with those who deny it any value.

tamil:
இணர்எரி தோய்வன்ன இன்னா செயினும்
புணரின் வெகுளாமை நன்று.
transliteration:
Inar eri thoivanna innaa seyinum
Punarin vekulaamai nandru.
current_meaning: Even if someone hurts you as badly as throwing you into a blazing fire, it is good, if you possibly can, not to get angry with them.
elementary: Sometimes people are so mean it feels like being burned. The kural says: even then, if you can, try not to become angry back. It is really hard, but it is the best and bravest thing to do.
university: This is the chapter's high-water mark of demand: inar eri, a fire of many clustered flames, is the image of the worst possible injury. The concessive punarin ('if it is possible', or in some readings 'if the offender seeks reconciliation') is realistic, acknowledging that non-anger in such extremity may exceed ordinary capacity, but it does not lower the ideal. Kalaignar's gloss takes punarin as the wrongdoer returning to seek friendship, making the couplet about accepting reconciliation without resentment. Either way, the teaching approaches the most radical ethics of non-retaliation found across traditions.

tamil:
உள்ளிய தெல்லாம் உடனெய்தும் உள்ளத்தால்
உள்ளான் வெகுளி எனின்.
transliteration:
Ulliyadhellaam udaneydhum ullaththaal
Ullaan vekuli enin.
current_meaning: If a person never lets even a thought of anger into their mind, they will right away get everything they hope for.
elementary: When your mind isn't full of angry thoughts, it has lots of room for good ideas and plans. People also like to help calm, kind people. So a mind without anger can reach its goals much more easily.
university: The couplet plays on the root ul- ('to think', 'the mind'): ulliyadhu ('what one has thought of'), ullaththaal ('in the mind'), and ullaan ('does not think of'). Valluvar sets the standard at the level of thought itself: it is not enough to avoid angry acts or words; one must not entertain (ullaan) anger inwardly. The promised reward, attaining all one intends 'at once' (udan), is striking, and commentators variously read it as worldly success (a clear mind and goodwill from others) or spiritual attainment. The couplet thus links inner purity from anger to efficacy in the world, a pattern also found in the Gita's promise of liberation for those free of desire and anger.

tamil:
இறந்தார் இறந்தார் அனையர் சினத்தைத்
துறந்தார் துறந்தார் துணை.
transliteration:
Irandhaar irandhaar anaiyar sinaththaith
Thurandhaar thurandhaar thunai.
current_meaning: People who let their anger go beyond all limits are as good as dead. People who have given up anger completely are as great as holy people who have left the world behind.
elementary: A person who is always furious is like someone who isn't really alive: there's no joy, kindness, or peace inside. But a person who has given up anger is like a wise holy person. Letting go of anger makes you truly alive.
university: The closing couplet is a celebrated piece of Tamil wordplay built on two repeated verbs. Irandhaar can mean 'those who have exceeded (all limits)' and 'those who have died'; thurandhaar can mean 'those who have renounced (anger)' and 'those who have renounced (the world)', that is, ascetics. Hence: the excessively angry are like the dead; those who give up anger equal the renunciants. Solomon Pappaiah's gloss offers an alternative reading, that those free of anger are like those who have escaped death, which neatly mirrors the first line. Placed in the Thuravaraviyal (the section on ascetic virtue), the couplet makes giving up anger itself a form of renunciation available to everyone.

tamil:
சிறப்பீனும் செல்வம் பெறினும் பிறர்க்குஇன்னா
செய்யாமை மாசற்றார் கோள்.
transliteration:
Sirappeenum selvam perinum pirarkku innaa
Seyyaamai maasatraar kol.
current_meaning: Even if hurting someone would bring them great riches and fame, people with pure minds keep firmly to their rule of never causing pain to others.
elementary: Imagine someone offers you a huge treasure chest, but only if you push another kid down to get it. A truly good person says “no thanks” every time. Valluvar says the pure-hearted never hurt anyone, not even for the biggest prize in the world.
university: The chapter opens by testing the principle of non-harm against its strongest temptation: sirappu eenum selvam, wealth that “gives birth to” distinction and social standing. The word kol (settled principle, fixed resolve) matters: non-harm is presented not as a mood or a calculation but as a standing commitment of the maasatraar, “those without stain,” whose minds are clear of the anger and greed that make harm seem attractive. Placed in the turavaraviyal (the section on the renunciant’s virtues), the couplet implies that the refusal to profit from another’s suffering is a defining mark of spiritual maturity, not merely of good manners. The same structure appears in Cicero’s Stoic claim that profiting by a neighbour’s loss is more contrary to nature than death or poverty, and in Plato’s thought-experiment of the Ring of Gyges, which asks whether anyone would stay just if injustice were profitable and safe. Valluvar’s answer is that the stainless would.

tamil:
கறுத்துஇன்னா செய்தவக் கண்ணும் மறுத்தின்னா
செய்யாமை மாசற்றார் கோள்.
transliteration:
Karuththu innaa seydhavak kannum maruththu innaa
Seyyaamai maasatraar kol.
current_meaning: Even when someone hurts them out of hate, people with pure minds make it their rule not to hurt that person back.
elementary: If a kid on the playground knocks over your sandcastle on purpose, it is tempting to knock over theirs too. This kural says good-hearted people don’t pay back hurt with more hurt, even when the other person started it.
university: Where Kural 311 tested non-harm against greed, 312 tests it against the stronger pull of justified grievance. Karuththu describes the other party’s grudging, hostile intent, while maruththu (in return, in retort) names the retaliatory impulse the stainless decline. The couplet repeats the closing phrase of 311 word for word (seyyaamai maasatraar kol), binding the two into a pair: neither profit nor provocation licenses harm. This places Valluvar alongside Socrates in the Crito, who startled his friend by insisting that one must not return injury for injury, and alongside the Sermon on the Mount and the Buddha’s Simile of the Saw. It also stands in contrast to the older Greek ethic of helping friends and harming enemies, which Plato’s Socrates set out to dismantle.

tamil:
செய்யாமல் செற்றார்க்கும் இன்னாத செய்தபின்
உய்யா விழுமந் தரும்.
transliteration:
Seyyaamal setraarkkum innaadha seydhapin
Uyyaa vizhumam tharum.
current_meaning: Even if people hate and hurt you when you did nothing to them, hurting them back will later bring you sorrow you cannot escape.
elementary: Suppose someone is mean to you for no reason at all, and you get them back. It might feel fair for a minute, but later you end up feeling awful and stuck in a big fight. The kural says hitting back, even when you didn’t start it, brings trouble you can’t get out of.
university: This couplet sharpens 312 by removing every excuse: the victim did nothing (seyyaamal) to provoke the enmity (setraar, those who hate). Even so, retaliating yields uyyaa vizhumam, a grief from which there is no escape. Because the chapter belongs to the section on the renunciant, older commentators and Pope’s translation read it as addressed to the ascetic, for whom retaliation undoes the discipline of years; the ‘inescapable sorrow’ is at once moral self-damage and the karmic consequence of the act. The logic is prudential as well as ethical: revenge draws the avenger into the cycle of harm. Greek tragedy dramatises exactly this spiral in the house of Atreus, and the Gospel compresses it into the saying that those who take the sword perish by it.

tamil:
இன்னாசெய் தாரை ஒறுத்தல் அவர்நாண
நன்னயஞ் செய்து விடல்.
transliteration:
Innaa seydhaarai oruththal avar naana
Nannayam seydhu vidal.
current_meaning: The best way to punish people who hurt you is to be so kind to them that they feel ashamed, and then to let the matter go.
elementary: If your brother breaks your toy and you share your snack with him anyway, he will probably feel really sorry about the toy. Valluvar says that is the best “punishment”: being so kind that the person feels ashamed of being mean, and then forgetting about it.
university: Perhaps the most quoted couplet of the chapter, 314 redefines punishment itself. Oruththal (to punish, chastise) is kept as the goal, but the means is nannayam (goodness, benefit), and its effect is naanam, the wrongdoer’s shame. The closing word vidal (to leave off, let go) led Parimelazhagar and later commentators such as Mu. Varadarasan to read the couplet as requiring one to forget both the injury received and the good returned, so that the kindness does not become a hidden weapon. The idea is found across traditions: Proverbs and Paul speak of heaping coals of fire on an enemy’s head by feeding him, and the Qur’an promises that repelling evil with what is better can turn an enemy into a close friend. What Valluvar adds is the paradox that the gentlest act is the most effective sanction.

tamil:
அறிவினான் ஆகுவ துண்டோ பிறிதின்நோய்
தந்நோய்போல் போற்றாக் கடை.
transliteration:
Arivinaan aaguvadhu undo piridhin noy
Thannoy pol potraak kadai.
current_meaning: What good is all your learning if you do not feel another creature’s pain as your own and protect it from suffering?
elementary: You might know lots of facts, like all the planets or every dinosaur. But if your friend falls and scrapes their knee and you don’t care, what good are all those facts? Valluvar says being smart only matters if you feel other people’s hurt like it’s your own.
university: Valluvar here makes empathy the test of knowledge. Arivu (knowledge, understanding) is asked to justify itself, and the only acceptable answer is that it leads one to regard piridhin noy, the pain of another (piridhu can mean any other being, not only humans), as thannoy, one’s own pain. The verb potru (to guard, protect, cherish) makes the demand active: it is not enough to feel sympathy, one must protect the other from harm as one protects oneself. This anticipates a recurring theme in the Kural that learning without moral application is barren. Comparable ideas appear in the Bhagavad Gita’s claim that true knowledge produces equal vision of all beings, in the Buddha’s reflection that since everyone holds themselves dear no one should harm another, and in the Stoic doctrine of oikeiosis, which asks us to draw the circle of concern outward until strangers are treated as kin.

tamil:
இன்னா எனத்தான் உணர்ந்தவை துன்னாமை
வேண்டும் பிறன்கண் செயல்.
transliteration:
Innaa enaththaan unarndhavai thunnaamai
Vendum piran kan seyal.
current_meaning: Whatever you have learned is painful from your own experience, never do that to anyone else.
elementary: Remember how much it hurt when someone left you out of a game? Then you already know not to leave anyone else out. This kural says: if something hurt you, don’t do it to others.
university: This is Valluvar’s clearest statement of the negative Golden Rule, and it is regularly cited alongside Hillel and the Mahabharata in comparative discussions of that principle. The phrase thaan unarndhavai, ‘what one has oneself felt or known,’ grounds the rule in lived experience rather than abstract principle: each person’s own suffering is a textbook of what not to do. Thunnaamai (not approaching, not engaging in) makes the prohibition wide enough to cover even drawing near to such acts. Unlike the positive form (‘do unto others’), the negative form sets a minimum that anyone can meet, and so needs no guesswork about what others want. It closely matches Brihaspati’s summary of dharma in the Mahabharata, Hillel’s one-sentence Torah, and Isocrates’ advice to the Cyprians.

tamil:
எனைத்தானும் எஞ்ஞான்றும் யார்க்கும் மனத்தானாம்
மாணாசெய் யாமை தலை.
transliteration:
Enaiththaanum ennaandrum yaarkkum manaththaanaam
Maanaa seyyaamai thalai.
current_meaning: The highest goodness is never to do anything low or hurtful to anyone, however small, at any time, not even in your thoughts.
elementary: Some people only stop themselves from hitting. This kural asks for much more: don’t hurt anyone, not a little bit, not ever, and don’t even plan mean things in your head. That, it says, is the very best kind of goodness.
university: The couplet universalises the prohibition along every axis at once: degree (enaiththaanum, in any measure however small), time (ennaandrum, at any time), and person (yaarkkum, to anyone). The fourth axis is inward: manaththaan aam, ‘that which arises from the mind,’ which commentators read either as deliberate, knowing harm or as harm committed even in intention. Maanaa means base or ignoble acts. Calling this thalai (the head, the foremost virtue) places total non-harm at the top of the chapter’s ethical hierarchy. Similar demands to extend the prohibition into the inner life appear in Leviticus’ command not to hate one’s brother in the heart, in the First Letter of John, where hatred is equated with murder, and in the Metta Sutta’s wish that no one should even desire harm for another.

tamil:
தன்னுயிர்க்கு இன்னாமை தானறிவான் என்கொலோ
மன்னுயிர்க்கு இன்னா செயல்.
transliteration:
Thannuyirkku innaamai thaan arivaan en kolo
Mannuyirkku innaa seyal.
current_meaning: A person knows well how pain feels in their own life. So why do they cause that same pain to other living beings?
elementary: You know how much a bee sting hurts, because it happened to you. So why would anyone go around stinging others? This kural asks: if you know how pain feels, how can you give it to someone else?
university: Kural 318 turns the rule of 316 into a question, and the rhetorical form (en kolo, ‘why, then?’) exposes a contradiction in the person who harms. The contrast between thannuyir (one’s own life or self) and mannuyir (the lives that dwell on earth, all living beings) widens the circle beyond humans, in keeping with the Kural’s broad concern for all creatures, developed further in the next chapter on not killing. The argument is essentially one of consistency: whoever knows pain from the inside cannot claim not to know what they are doing when they cause it. Similar appeals to self-knowledge appear in the Gita’s ‘comparison to one’s own self,’ the Dhammapada’s instruction to put oneself in another’s place, and the Torah’s reminder that Israel knows the heart of the stranger because it was once a stranger.

tamil:
பிறர்க்கின்னா முற்பகல் செய்யின் தமக்குஇன்னா
பிற்பகல் தாமே வரும்.
transliteration:
Pirarkku innaa murpagal seyyin thamakku innaa
Pirpagal thaame varum.
current_meaning: If you harm others in the morning, harm will come back to you on its own by the afternoon.
elementary: It’s like throwing a ball hard against a wall: it bounces right back at you. This kural says being mean to someone in the morning means trouble will come bouncing back to you by the afternoon.
university: This is among the best-known couplets in Tamil, often quoted as a proverb. Its power lies in its compression of time: murpagal (forenoon) and pirpagal (afternoon) shrink the karmic interval, usually imagined across lifetimes, to a single day. The word thaame (of their own accord) makes the return automatic; no avenger or judge is named, and the consequence seems built into the act. The couplet thus combines a moral law with a psychological one, since harm tends to provoke retaliation and hostility quickly. Parallels range from the Mahabharata’s observation that the injured turns round and injures the injurer, to Proverbs’ image of the stone that rolls back on the one who pushes it, to Theseus giving each bandit on the road to Athens the death he dealt to others.

tamil:
நோயெல்லாம் நோய்செய்தார் மேலவாம் நோய்செய்யார்
நோயின்மை வேண்டு பவர்.
transliteration:
Noyellaam noy seydhaar melavaam noy seyyaar
Noyinmai vendu pavar.
current_meaning: All suffering comes back to those who cause suffering. So people who want to be free of suffering do not cause it to others.
elementary: If you plant thorns, you will get pricked walking through your own garden. If you never want to get pricked, don’t plant thorns. This kural says: if you want a life without pain, don’t give pain to anyone.
university: The chapter closes with a verbal tour de force: the word noy (pain, affliction, disease) appears four times in seven words, so that the sound of the couplet enacts its argument that pain circles back to its source. The first line states a law (all affliction settles on those who afflict), and the second draws the practical conclusion for anyone who wants noyinmai, freedom from suffering. The ethics of non-harm is here grounded partly in enlightened self-interest, rounding off a chapter that has moved from the stainless person’s principle (311–312), through empathy (315–318), to consequence (319–320). The idea is widely shared: Hesiod’s warning that the evil plotter harms himself most, the Qur’an’s statement that evil plotting backfires on the plotters, Marcus Aurelius’ remark that the wrongdoer wrongs himself, and the Dhammapada’s assurance that for one who does no evil there is no ill.

tamil:
அறவினை யாதெனின் கொல்லாமை கோறல்
பிறவினை எல்லாந் தரும்.
transliteration:
Aravinai yaadhenin kollaamai koral
Piravinai ellaam tharum.
current_meaning: If you ask what doing good means, it is not killing any living thing. Killing brings every other kind of evil deed along with it.
elementary: Imagine a row of dominoes. If you knock over the first one, all the others fall too. Valluvar says killing is that first domino: once someone is willing to take a life, every other bad act becomes easy. Not killing keeps the whole row standing.
university: Valluvar answers the question “what is aram (virtue)?” with a single negative act — kollaamai, abstention from killing — and then gives its mirror image: kōṟal (killing) “yields all other deeds” (piṟavinai), which the classical commentators, including Mu. Varadarasan, read as all non-virtuous deeds. The couplet therefore makes non-killing not merely one virtue among many but the generative root of the moral life, with killing as the root of vice. This places the Kural squarely within the broad śramaṇic and Brahmanical consensus of early-first-millennium India that ahiṃsā is the highest dharma, a position shared by Jain, Buddhist and epic Hindu sources. The structure of the verse — definition followed by its contrary — is typical of Valluvar’s aphoristic logic, compressing an entire ethical theory into seven words.

tamil:
பகுத்துண்டு பல்லுயிர் ஓம்புதல் நூலோர்
தொகுத்தவற்றுள் எல்லாந் தலை.
transliteration:
Pakuththundu palluyir oampudhal nooloar
Thokuththavatrul ellaam thalai.
current_meaning: Sharing your food with others and protecting all kinds of living things is the greatest of all the good deeds that wise writers have listed in their books.
elementary: If you have a lunchbox and a hungry friend, you split your sandwich. If you see a bird with a hurt wing, you help it. Valluvar says that sharing and taking care of every living thing is the number-one rule in all the good books ever written.
university: The couplet fuses two duties — sharing food (pakuttuṇṭal) and protecting the manifold life of creatures (palluyir ōmputal) — and ranks them as “the head” (talai) of everything the authors of moral treatises (nūlōr) have compiled. Its placement in the chapter on non-killing shows that for Valluvar non-violence is not merely a prohibition but has a positive face: actively sustaining life. The appeal to the collected wisdom of the nūlōr is also a characteristic move, presenting the Kural as a distillation of an entire ethical literature. The pairing of generosity and care for life anticipates modern ethics of care that see nurture, not only abstention from harm, as the core of morality.

tamil:
ஒன்றாக நல்லது கொல்லாமை மற்றதன்
பின்சாரப் பொய்யாமை நன்று.
transliteration:
Ondraaka nalladhu kollaamai matradhan
Pinsaarap poiyaamai nandru.
current_meaning: Not killing stands alone as the greatest good. Right behind it, in second place, comes not lying.
elementary: Think of a race where first prize is gold and second is silver. Valluvar gives the gold medal to “never kill” and the silver medal to “never lie.” Both are winners, but not hurting any living thing comes first.
university: Here Valluvar explicitly ranks two virtues he has treated separately: kollaamai (non-killing) is good “as one” (oṉṟāka) — unique and incomparable — and poyyāmai (truthfulness, the subject of chapter 30) is good “following behind it.” This is notable because in chapter 30 he had praised truth in superlative terms; the commentators reconcile the two by saying truth is supreme among virtues of speech, but non-killing is supreme absolutely. The ordering precisely mirrors Patañjali’s list of yamas, where ahiṃsā precedes satya, and the Buddhist precepts, where abstaining from killing is first and false speech fourth. It also contrasts with Gandhi, who, while treating the two as inseparable, made Truth the end and ahimsa the means.

tamil:
நல்லாறு எனப்படுவது யாதெனின் யாதொன்றும்
கொல்லாமை சூழும் நெறி.
transliteration:
Nallaaru enappaduvadhu yaadhenin yaadhondrum
Kollaamai soozhum neri.
current_meaning: If you ask what the good path is, it is the way of life that takes care never to kill any creature at all.
elementary: When you walk in a garden, you watch where you step so you don’t squash the ants or crush the flowers. Valluvar says the “good road” in life is exactly that: always looking out so that you don’t hurt even the smallest living thing.
university: The couplet defines nallāṟu, “the good path,” not by a doctrine or ritual but by a disposition: the neṟi (way of conduct) that “deliberates upon” (cūḻum) not killing “anything at all” (yātoṉṟum). The verb cūḻ suggests active, careful forethought — non-killing is not passive but a vigilant attentiveness in every act. The phrase yātoṉṟum explicitly extends the scope to all living beings, however small, aligning the Kural with the rigorous ahiṃsā of Jain and Buddhist ethics. This conception of ethics as an attentive way of moving through the world anticipates Albert Schweitzer’s “reverence for life.”

tamil:
நிலைஅஞ்சி நீத்தாருள் எல்லாம் கொலைஅஞ்சிக்
கொல்லாமை சூழ்வான் தலை.
transliteration:
Nilaianji neeththaarul ellaam kolaianjik
Kollaamai soozhvaan thalai.
current_meaning: Many people give up the world because they fear the endless cycle of life and death. The greatest of them is the one who fears the wrong of killing and carefully keeps from it.
elementary: Some people give up their toys, their fancy food and their comfy beds to become monks. That’s hard! But Valluvar says the very best of them is the one who is most careful never to hurt a living thing. Being gentle matters more than giving things up.
university: Valluvar compares two kinds of fear: nilai añci — fear of the “state” of worldly existence and rebirth that drives ascetics to renounce (nīttār) — and kolai añci, fear of the guilt of killing. He declares that among all renunciants, the one moved by the second fear and who deliberates on non-killing is talai, the head. This subordinates the whole apparatus of asceticism to a single ethical commitment, a characteristic Kural move that ranks inner moral conduct over outward religious status. The same move appears in the Mahabharata’s claim that ahimsa is itself the highest penance, and in the Dhammapada’s definition of the true monk as one who has laid down violence toward all beings.

tamil:
கொல்லாமை மேற்கொண் டொழுகுவான் வாழ்நாள்மேல்
செல்லாது உயிருண்ணுங் கூற்று.
transliteration:
Kollaamai merkon dozhuguvaan vaazhnaalmel
Sellaadhu uyirunnum kootru.
current_meaning: Death, which eats up all lives, will not come to cut short the days of someone who has made not killing the rule they live by.
elementary: In old stories, Death is like a hunter who comes to take people away. Valluvar says that hunter holds back from someone who never hurts any creature — as if even Death respects a person who protects life.
university: Kūṟṟu, “the one who divides” (Yama, Death), is here personified as “the eater of lives” (uyiruṇṇum). Valluvar claims that it “will not go” (cellātu) against the life-span of one who lives by non-killing. Commentators differ: some read this literally as a promise of long life, others (like Kalaignar) as a poetic image of Death hesitating in awe, and still others spiritually, as freedom from the cycle of rebirth. The idea of karmic reciprocity — sparing life earns life — is explicit in Buddhist teaching on the karmic causes of long and short lives, and has echoes in the biblical promise of prolonged days for sparing the mother bird.

tamil:
தன்னுயிர் நீப்பினும் செய்யற்க தான்பிறிது
இன்னுயிர் நீக்கும் வினை.
transliteration:
Thannuyir neeppinum seyyarka thaanpiridhu
Innuyir neekkum vinai.
current_meaning: Even if it costs you your own life, do not do anything that takes away the precious life of another being.
elementary: Suppose a bully says, “Hurt that puppy or I’ll hurt you.” Valluvar says: don’t hurt the puppy, even if you get hurt yourself. The puppy’s life is just as sweet to it as yours is to you.
university: This is one of the most uncompromising couplets in the Kural: one must not perform “the act that removes another’s sweet life” (piṟitu iṉṉuyir nīkkum viṉai) even if it means losing one’s own. The adjective iṉ (sweet) applied to the other’s life insists on its equal preciousness. Varadarasan explicitly reads it as forbidding killing even to save oneself — a stance close to Jain absolutism and more radical than most legal traditions, which permit self-defence. The Talmud reaches a similar conclusion for the case of being forced to kill an innocent person under threat, reasoning that one cannot know one’s own blood is “redder” than another’s.

tamil:
நன்றாகும் ஆக்கம் பெரிதெனினும் சான்றோர்க்குக்
கொன்றாகும் ஆக்கங் கடை.
transliteration:
Nandraakum aakkam peridheninum saandrorkkuk
Kondraakum aakkam kadai.
current_meaning: Even if people say the gain from killing is great and good, good-hearted people see any gain that comes from killing as the lowest of things.
elementary: Imagine someone says, “If you trap and kill this bird, you’ll win a huge prize.” A good person says “No, thanks.” Valluvar says a prize that costs a life isn’t a prize at all — it’s the worst kind of win.
university: Valluvar concedes his opponent’s premise — the prosperity (ākkam) gained may indeed be “great” and even called “good” — and still pronounces it kaṭai, the very lowest, in the eyes of the cāṉṟōr (the noble, perfected ones). Parimelazhagar and Solomon Pappaiah read the verse as targeting Vedic animal sacrifice (vēḷvi), which promised wealth and heaven through ritual killing; the Kural thus sides with the Jain and Buddhist critique of sacrificial violence. More broadly the couplet rejects consequentialist justifications for killing: no outcome, however beneficial, can redeem the means. The same refusal to let ends justify the taking of life underlies Kant’s formula that persons may never be used merely as means.

tamil:
கொலைவினைய ராகிய மாக்கள் புலைவினையர்
புன்மை தெரிவா ரகத்து.
transliteration:
Kolaivinaiya raagiya maakkal pulaivinaiyar
Punmai therivaa ragaththu.
current_meaning: People who kill for a living are seen as doers of shameful deeds by those who understand what truly low behavior is.
elementary: Some jobs make you proud, like helping people or growing food. Valluvar says that a job built on killing living things makes wise people think less of you, because they can see how it hardens the heart.
university: The couplet names the kolaiviṉaiyar, those whose “occupation” (viṉai) is killing, and uses the word mākkaḷ — often reserved for people who have lost human discernment — to describe them. In the minds of those who discern baseness (puṉmai terivār), they are pulaiviṉaiyar, doers of polluted, degraded work. The verse is a moral judgement rather than a caste statement, though the vocabulary of pulai (pollution) reflects the social idiom of its time and should be read critically today. Its underlying insight — that habitual killing corrodes compassion — is shared by the Buddha’s list of wrong livelihoods and by Thomas More’s Utopians, who kept citizens from butchery lest it destroy the feeling of mercy.

tamil:
உயிருடம்பின் நீக்கியா ரென்ப செயிருடம்பின்
செல்லாத்தீ வாழ்க்கை யவர்.
transliteration:
Uyirudambin neekkiyaa renba seyirudambin
Sellaaththee vaazhkkai yavar.
current_meaning: Wise people say that those who now live poor, miserable lives in sick bodies are the ones who once took the lives of other beings.
elementary: It’s like planting seeds: if you plant thorns, you get thorns later. Valluvar says that hurting and killing are like planting thorn seeds — sooner or later, sickness and hard times grow back toward the one who planted them.
university: The final couplet adopts the voice of received wisdom (eṉpa, “they say”): those with diseased bodies (ceyir uṭampu) living a miserable, impoverished life (cellāt tī vāḻkkai) are those who “removed life from bodies” (uyir uṭampiṉ nīkkiyār). All the major commentators read this karmically, as the fruit of killing in a former birth. The couplet closes the chapter by grounding the ethics of non-killing in moral causation; it has parallels in Manu and in the Buddha’s teaching that harming beings leads to sickliness. Modern readers will note that such teaching can be misused to blame the sick and poor — a danger also recognised within other traditions, as when Jesus rejects the idea that a man’s blindness was caused by sin (John 9:3).

tamil:
நில்லாத வற்றை நிலையின என்றுணரும்
புல்லறி வாண்மை கடை.
transliteration:
Nillaadha vatrai nilaiyina endru unarum
Pullarivu aanmai kadai.
current_meaning: Believing that things which cannot last will last forever is the worst kind of foolishness.
elementary: Imagine building a sandcastle and believing it will stay on the beach forever, even though the waves always come. This kural says that treating things that will surely change or go away as if they will last forever is the silliest mistake a person can make.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter on impermanence not with a description of transience but with an epistemic judgement: the root error is a false cognition, mistaking the non-abiding (nillaadhavai) for the abiding (nilaiyina). The phrase “pullarivaanmai” (petty-mindedness, a paltry intelligence that presumes itself competent) frames the problem as a defect of understanding rather than of morals, and “kadai” (the lowest, the most base) ranks it at the bottom of human conditions. Commentators from Parimelazhagar onward read the chapter as the doorway of the renunciate section (thuravaraviyal), since recognising impermanence (nilaiyaamai) is what loosens attachment and makes renunciation (the next chapter, thuravu) intelligible.
