The idea sits close to the Buddhist and Jain analysis of avidya/moha, where suffering follows from treating the impermanent as permanent, and to the Stoic insistence that disturbance comes from our judgements about things rather than from the things themselves.

tamil:
கூத்தாட்டு அவைக்குழாத் தற்றே பெருஞ்செல்வம்
போக்கும் அதுவிளிந் தற்று.
transliteration:
Koothaattu avaikkuzhaath thatre perunjelvam
Pokkum adhu vilindhatru.
current_meaning: Great riches come together like a crowd gathering to watch a show, and they leave like that crowd going home when the show is over.
elementary: Think of people crowding in to watch a street show. When the show ends, everyone walks away at once and the place is empty. This kural says money is like that crowd: it comes in bit by bit, and it can leave all at once.
university: Valluvar builds the couplet on a single theatrical simile with two halves: the assembling of an audience (koothaattu avaik kuzhaam) and its dispersal when the performance ends (adhu vilindhatru). Commentators note the asymmetry the image implies: an audience trickles in gradually but leaves together, just as wealth is accumulated slowly and can vanish in a single reversal. The theatre is also suggestive, since the crowd was never attached to the patron but to the spectacle, much as wealth is never truly bound to its holder. The kural therefore relocates wealth from the category of possession to that of event, something that happens around a person for a time. Comparable ideas appear in the Greek theme of the reversal of fortune (Solon and Croesus) and in the Stoic teaching that external goods are on loan.

tamil:
அற்கா இயல்பிற்றுச் செல்வம் அதுபெற்றால்
அற்குப ஆங்கே செயல்.
transliteration:
Arkaa iyalbitruch selvam adhu petraal
Arkupa aange seyal.
current_meaning: Riches never stay for long. So when you have them, use them right away to do good deeds that will last.
elementary: If you are given ice cream on a hot day, you should share it right away before it melts. This kural says money is like that ice cream: it won't stay, so use it for good things now, while you still have it.
university: The couplet turns on a deliberate play between “arkaa” (that which does not stay) and “arkupa” (things that do stay, that is, enduring deeds), both drawn from the verb ‘ar’, to abide. Valluvar thus converts a descriptive claim about wealth into an imperative: since wealth is non-abiding, use it for what abides, and do so “aange” (then and there, at once). Commentators identify the enduring deeds with the householder virtues discussed earlier in the work, such as hospitality, charity and helpfulness (oppuravu). The logic is an ethical economics: a perishable asset should be exchanged immediately for an imperishable one before it spoils. The same move, turning transient riches into lasting merit, appears in the Gospel's ‘treasures in heaven’, the Quran's ‘enduring good deeds’, and Bhartrhari's teaching that wealth has only three destinies.

tamil:
நாளென ஒன்றுபோற் காட்டி உயிர்ஈரும்
வாளது உணர்வார்ப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
Naal ena ondru pol kaatti uyir eerum
Vaal adhu unarvaar perin.
current_meaning: A day looks like just a stretch of time. But people who understand know it is really a saw, cutting away at your life bit by bit.
elementary: Each day feels like just another day: you wake up, play, and sleep. But every day that passes is one less day you have left, like a saw slowly cutting through a log. This kural says wise people notice this.
university: The couplet turns on an unmasking: “naal” (the day) displays itself (kaatti) as a neutral thing, an ordinary measure of time, but its real nature is a “vaal” (blade, commonly understood as a saw) that “eerum” (cleaves, saws through) life. The verb eer suggests the slow back-and-forth of a saw rather than a single cut, so life is shown being worn away in daily strokes. The conditional “unarvaarp perin” (if one finds those who understand) implies that such people are rare; most take the passing day at face value. Philosophically the kural anticipates Seneca's remark that we die daily and the Psalmist's prayer to ‘number our days’: time is not a container in which life takes place, but the very process by which life is used up.

tamil:
நாச்செற்று விக்குள்மேல் வாராமுன் நல்வினை
மேற்சென்று செய்யப் படும்.
transliteration:
Naachchetru vikkul mel vaaraamun nalvinai
Mersendru seyyap padum.
current_meaning: Before your tongue stops working and the death rattle (the last breathing sound of a dying person) rises in your throat, hurry to do good deeds.
elementary: If you want to say sorry or help someone, don't wait for ‘someday’, because someday might not come. This kural says do your good deeds now, while you still can talk and act.
university: Valluvar gives the chapter's abstract point a stark physical image: “naa chetru” (the tongue locked or stilled) and “vikkul mel vaaraa mun” (before the hiccup, the death rattle, rises), which are the classical signs of the last moments of life. The imperative “mersendru” (going forward, pressing ahead) carries the sense of taking the initiative and not waiting for circumstances. The image of a silenced tongue also implies that at the end one cannot even speak one's intentions, let alone carry them out. The kural thus moves from recognising impermanence to acting urgently, an ethic of timeliness found in Rabbi Eliezer's ‘repent one day before your death’, the Quran's warning against wishing for a reprieve at death, and Marcus Aurelius' ‘while it is in thy power, be good’.

tamil:
நெருநல் உளனொருவன் இன்றில்லை என்னும்
பெருமை உடைத்துஇவ் வுலகு.
transliteration:
Nerunal ulan oruvan indru illai ennum
Perumai udaiththu ivvulagu.
current_meaning: This world has a strange kind of greatness: someone who was here yesterday is gone today.
elementary: Sometimes we hear, ‘I just saw him yesterday, and now he's gone.’ This kural says that is simply how the world works: people can be here one day and gone the next.
university: The couplet is famous for its irony. “Perumai” (greatness, glory) is normally praise, but Valluvar awards it to the world for the most unsettling of distinctions, that a man alive “nerunal” (yesterday) is not there “indru” (today). Commentators such as the thirukkural-thamizh gloss explicitly read perumai here as a mocking word for the world's instability. The unit of time is only a single day, which heightens the sense of suddenness. The world's one reliable ‘achievement’ is the constant disappearance of its inhabitants. The observation echoes the Yaksha's question in the Mahabharata about the wonder of human denial of death, and Marcus Aurelius' remark about yesterday's mucus becoming tomorrow's ashes.

tamil:
ஒருபொழுதும் வாழ்வது அறியார் கருதுப
கோடியும் அல்ல பல.
transliteration:
Oru pozhudhum vaazhvadhu ariyaar karudhupa
Kodiyum alla pala.
current_meaning: People cannot know if they will live even one more moment, yet they make countless plans, more than ten million of them.
elementary: Someone might plan what they'll do next week, next year, and in ten years, even though nobody knows for sure what will happen tomorrow. This kural gently laughs at how many plans we make when we can't even be sure of the next hour.
university: The couplet's force comes from the mismatch of scale: “oru pozhudhu” (a single moment or watch of the day) against “kodiyum alla pala” (not a crore, i.e. ten million, but more). People who cannot guarantee a single stretch of time still carry countless projects, desires and calculations. Commentators note the progression within the chapter from “yesterday/today” (336) to an even smaller unit, “one moment” (337), tightening the frame of uncertainty. The critique is not of planning as such but of a mind that lives in imagined futures while forgetting its own fragility. The Gita's portrait of the deluded man counting his gains ‘today’ and ‘tomorrow’, Jesus' parable of the rich fool, and Aeschylus' ‘blind hopes’ all diagnose the same condition.

tamil:
குடம்பை தனித்துஒழியப் புள்பறந் தற்றே
உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை நட்பு.
transliteration:
Kudambai thaniththu ozhiyap pul parandhatre
Udambodu uyiridai natpu.
current_meaning: The friendship between the body and the soul is like a bird that flies away and leaves its egg (or nest) behind, empty and alone.
elementary: A baby bird grows inside an egg, but one day it breaks out and flies off, leaving the empty shell behind. This kural says our life and our body are like that: one day life flies off, and the body is left behind like the shell.
university: The meaning turns on the word “kudambai”, which Parimelazhagar and many commentators gloss as ‘egg’ (so the chick breaks out and leaves the shell), while others read it as ‘nest’ (so a grown bird abandons its home); both readings agree that the container is left “thaniththu ozhiya” (abandoned, alone). Calling the relationship “natpu” (friendship) is pointed, since it is a friendship of convenience that ends the moment the occupant departs. The egg reading adds the idea that the body was the soul's place of formation, not its permanent home, which prepares for kural 340. The image of soul and body as distinct, one of them leaving the other, parallels the Gita's worn-out garments, Ecclesiastes' spirit returning to God, and Plato's definition of death in the Phaedo as the separation of soul from body.

tamil:
உறங்கு வதுபோலுஞ் சாக்காடு உறங்கி
விழிப்பது போலும் பிறப்பு.
transliteration:
Urangu vadhu polum saakkaadu urangi
Vizhippadhu polum pirappu.
current_meaning: Death is like falling asleep, and being born is like waking up after sleep.
elementary: Every night you fall asleep, and every morning you wake up again. This kural says dying is like falling asleep, and being born is like waking up.
university: The couplet is the chapter's most compressed statement: “saakkaadu” (death) is like “uranguvadhu” (sleeping), and “pirappu” (birth) is like “urangi vizhippadhu” (waking after sleep). Most traditional commentators read it within the Indian framework of rebirth: death and birth follow one another as naturally as sleep and waking, so the cycle is familiar rather than terrifying, and the real goal is to escape it (veedu). Some modern readers, including Kalaignar's gloss, take a more secular line, stressing that death is a sleep from which one does not wake. The analogy is found across traditions: the Greek twins Hypnos and Thanatos, Socrates' ‘dreamless sleep’, the biblical ‘those who sleep in the dust’ shall awake, and the Quran's teaching that God takes souls both in death and in sleep.

tamil:
புக்கில் அமைந்தின்று கொல்லோ உடம்பினுள்
துச்சில் இருந்த உயிர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Pukkil amaindhindru kollo udambinul
Thuchchil irundha uyirkku.
current_meaning: The soul only stays for a while in a corner of the body. It seems it has not yet found a lasting home of its own.
elementary: Imagine a traveller who keeps staying in borrowed rooms, moving from one to the next, never having a house of their own. This kural says the soul is like that traveller: the body is only a temporary room, and it is still looking for its true home.
university: Valluvar closes the chapter with a question rather than a statement. “Pukkil” (a settled dwelling, a home one enters to stay) is contrasted with “thuchchil” (a temporary lodging, a borrowed corner), and the particle “kollo” (is it perhaps that...?) gives the line a tone of wondering. The soul is pictured as a tenant in a rented corner of the body, which explains why it keeps moving from body to body: it has not yet reached its true home, which traditional commentators identify with veedu (liberation). The chapter thus moves from wealth (332-333), to time (334-337), to the body (338-339), and finally to the homelessness of the soul, handing on to the next chapter on renunciation. Parallels include the Gita's ‘transient world’ from which liberated souls do not return, Paul's ‘earthly house of this tabernacle’, the hadith of being a ‘stranger or traveller’, and Marcus Aurelius' ‘stranger's sojourn’.

tamil:
யாதனின் யாதனின் நீங்கியான் நோதல்
அதனின் அதனின் இலன்.
transliteration:
Yaadhanin yaadhanin neengiyaan nodhal
Adhanin adhanin ilan.
current_meaning: Whatever a person has let go of, whatever it may be, that thing can no longer cause them pain.
elementary: If you stop caring about keeping a certain toy, you won't cry when it breaks. This kural says every single thing you stop clinging to is one less thing that can make you sad.
university: The doubled pronouns (yaadhanin yaadhanin … adhanin adhanin, “from whatever, whatever … from that, that”) set up an exact one-to-one ledger: each object released cancels the suffering tied to that particular object. Parimelazhagar reads the couplet as the gradualist justification for renunciation — one need not abandon everything at once to begin reaping relief, since each detachment pays its own dividend; Karunanidhi likewise glosses it as “whichever single attachment one gives up.” The chapter therefore opens not with an ascetic command but with a near-empirical observation about the mechanics of grief: pain travels along the line of attachment. The same causal claim underlies the Buddhist analysis of suffering as arising from clinging (upādāna) and the Stoic insistence that distress comes from our relation to externals rather than from the externals themselves.

tamil:
வேண்டின்உண் டாகத் துறக்க துறந்தபின்
ஈண்டுஇயற் பால பல.
transliteration:
Vendin undaagath thurakka thurandhapin
Eendu iyarpaala pala.
current_meaning: If you want lasting good, give things up while you still have them. Once you have given them up, many joys come to you even in this life.
elementary: Taking a heavy backpack off before a long hike isn't losing anything — it's how you get to enjoy the walk. This kural says give things up while you still have them, and you'll find lots of happiness right away.
university: The phrase undaaga (“while [they] exist”) is read by Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasan as a timing instruction: renounce while wealth, strength and opportunity are still in hand, not after they have already slipped away — giving up what one no longer has is not renunciation at all. The second line's eendu (“here”, in this world) is striking: Valluvar promises not only a post-mortem reward but many present goods (iyarpaala pala), countering the caricature of renunciation as pure deprivation. This anticipates the famous Upanishadic paradox that one enjoys by relinquishing. Placed after the Kural's earlier praise of the householder (ch. 5, Ilvaazhkai), the couplet presents thuravu as a voluntary, later-chosen stage rather than a universal command.

tamil:
அடல்வேண்டும் ஐந்தன் புலத்தை விடல்வேண்டும்
வேண்டிய வெல்லாம் ஒருங்கு.
transliteration:
Adalvendum aindhan pulaththai vidalvendum
Vendiya vellaam orungu.
current_meaning: You must control your five senses and, at the same time, give up all the things they crave.
elementary: Imagine five puppies each pulling you toward a different treat. You need to hold all five leashes AND put all the treats away. This kural says control all five senses and let go of everything they want, all at once.
university: The couplet is built on two parallel imperatives (adalvendum … vidalvendum, “must conquer … must abandon”): conquest of the five sense-fields (aindhan pulam — sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch) and the simultaneous relinquishing of all that they desire. The final word orungu (“together, all at once”) is decisive; Parimelazhagar stresses that a partial abandonment leaves a foothold from which desire regrows. Pairing inner control with outer relinquishment mirrors the Indic scheme of indriya-nigraha and tyaga, and recalls Kural 6's praise of the one who has quenched the five sense-gates. Across traditions the senses appear as the doorways through which the world lays claim to the self — the Gita's tortoise, Plato's unruly horse, Odysseus's wax-stopped crew.

tamil:
இயல்பாகும் நோன்பிற்கொன்று இன்மை உடைமை
மயலாகும் மற்றும் பெயர்த்து.
transliteration:
Iyalbaagum nonbirkondru inmai udaimai
Mayalaagum matrum peyarththu.
current_meaning: Owning nothing at all is natural for someone who has truly given up the world. Owning even one thing pulls them back into the false thinking they had left behind.
elementary: If you are trying to stop eating sweets, keeping 'just one piece' in your pocket makes it very hard to stop thinking about sweets. This kural says someone who has given things up should keep nothing, because even one thing can pull them back.
university: Inmai (having nothing) is called the iyalbu — the natural, defining character — of nonbu (austerity, tapas). The second line's peyarththu (“turning back, reversing”) suggests that possession does not merely distract but undoes progress, returning the renunciant to mayal, bewilderment; Karunanidhi glosses that even one attachment multiplies into many. This is a stricter standard than Kural 341's gradualism, and it applies specifically to one who has already taken up the ascetic life. Comparable rules shaped the Buddhist monk's short list of requisites, the Jain ideal of aparigraha, and the apostolic mission charge in Matthew 10; the Cynic Diogenes made the same point theatrically.

tamil:
மற்றும் தொடர்ப்பாடு எவன்கொல் பிறப்பறுக்கல்
உற்றார்க்கு உடம்பும் மிகை.
transliteration:
Matrum thodarppaadu evankol pirapparukkal
Utraarkku udambum migai.
current_meaning: For people working to end the cycle of being born again and again, even their own body is one thing too many. So why take on any more ties?
elementary: If you are trying to swim across a river, even your shoes feel heavy. Why would you carry a suitcase too? This kural says someone trying to be truly free finds even their own body a load, so they shouldn't add extra burdens.
university: The couplet argues a fortiori: if even the body — the one attachment that cannot simply be discarded — is migai (excess, surplus) to someone who has set out to cut off births (pirappu arukkal), then every additional bond (thodarppaadu) is indefensible. Parimelazhagar notes that the body is retained only as the instrument through which austerity is practised, not valued for its own sake. The verse does not counsel harming the body; it relocates the body from 'self' to 'tool'. The idea resonates with Plato's Phaedo, where philosophy is a rehearsal for the soul's release from the body, with Paul's groaning 'in this tabernacle', and with the Buddha's house-builder verse, in which the body is the house craving keeps rebuilding.

tamil:
யானென தென்னுஞ் செருக்கறுப்பான் வானோர்க்
குயர்ந்த உலகம் புகும்.
transliteration:
Yaanenadhu ennum serukkaruppaan vaanork
kuyarndha ulagam pugum.
current_meaning: A person who cuts away the pride of thinking “I” and “mine” will reach a world higher even than the world of the gods.
elementary: Imagine a kid who stops shouting 'Mine! Mine!' about every toy and stops acting like everything is about them. This kural says a person who drops 'me' and 'mine' reaches a place even better than heaven.
university: Yaan (“I”) and enadhu (“mine”) are the Tamil counterparts of ahankara and mamakara; Parimelazhagar glosses them as mistaking the body for the self and taking unconnected things as one's own, and calls this pairing serukku — pride or delusion. The reward, vaanorkku uyarndha ulagam (“a world higher than the gods'”), is read by traditional commentators as liberation (veedu), which lies beyond even the heavens, themselves impermanent. Karunanidhi, consistent with his rationalist reading, renders it instead as a renown surpassing heaven's. The couplet thus makes ego itself, not property, the root to be severed — property is simply 'mine' extended outward. The parallel with Gita 2.71 (nirmamo nirahankarah, 'without mine, without ego') is almost verbatim.

tamil:
பற்றி விடாஅ இடும்பைகள் பற்றினைப்
பற்றி விடாஅ தவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Patri vidaaa idumbaigal patrinaip
Patri vidaaa thavarkku.
current_meaning: Sorrows grab hold and never let go of people who hold tightly to the things they are attached to and will not let them go.
elementary: If you grab a cactus and refuse to let go, it keeps hurting you. This kural says when you hang on tightly to things, troubles hang on tightly to you.
university: One of the Kural's most celebrated pieces of wordplay: the phrase patri vidaaa (“seizing, not releasing”) appears twice, first describing sorrows (idumbaigal) and then describing people who hold on to patru (attachment). The mirror structure enacts the moral — the grip we exert is the grip exerted upon us. Mu. Varadarasan specifies the attachments as the twofold 'I' and 'mine' of the previous couplet, making this verse the causal explanation of Kural 346. The same self-reinforcing loop is analysed in Buddhist accounts of craving, in the Gita's chain from dwelling on objects to attachment to desire, and in Spinoza's description of human bondage to the passions.

tamil:
தலைப்பட்டார் தீரத் துறந்தார் மயங்கி
வலைப்பட்டார் மற்றை யவர்.
transliteration:
Thalaippattaar theerath thurandhaar mayangi
Valaippattaar matrai yavar.
current_meaning: People who have given up everything completely have reached the highest goal. All others are confused and caught in a net.
elementary: A fish that swims completely clear of the net stays free, but a fish that stays near it 'just a little' gets caught. This kural says people who give up everything are truly free, while the rest get tangled up.
university: Theera (“wholly, to the very end”) is the key word: Valluvar contrasts complete renunciants, who have thalaippattaar — 'reached the head', attained the goal — with the rest, who, bewildered (mayangi), are valaippattaar, 'netted'. The rhyming pair thalaippattaar/valaippattaar sharpens the stark binary. Commentators differ over the net: Parimelazhagar and Solomon Pappaiah take it as the net of repeated births, Mu. Varadarasan and Karunanidhi as the net of ignorance. The couplet refuses any comfortable middle position — a half-renunciation still counts as capture — in line with Luke 9:62's warning against looking back from the plough and the Gita's 'mesh of delusion'.

tamil:
பற்றற்ற கண்ணே பிறப்பறுக்கும் மற்று
நிலையாமை காணப் படும்.
transliteration:
Patratra kanne pirapparukkum matru
Nilaiyaamai kaanap padum.
current_meaning: The moment a person lets go of all attachments, the cycle of rebirth is cut. Otherwise, they keep going round and round in an endless, unsteady cycle of birth and death.
elementary: A spinning top keeps going as long as you keep flicking it; stop flicking, and it finally rests. This kural says once you stop clinging, the cycle of being born again and again stops — and if you don't, everything keeps wobbling and changing.
university: Kanne (“at that very point”) stresses immediacy: liberation coincides with the cessation of patru rather than following it as a later reward. The second line is read in two ways. Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasan take matru as 'otherwise': without detachment, instability — the alternation of births and deaths — will be seen. Puliyur Kesikan reads it as 'moreover': with detachment, the impermanence of the world is then clearly seen. Either way the couplet binds this chapter to the preceding one, Nilaiyaamai (Impermanence, ch. 34). The claim that the end of desire is the end of rebirth is shared almost word for word by the Katha Upanishad and the Dhammapada, and appears inverted in the Orphic hope of escaping the 'wheel'.

tamil:
பற்றுக பற்றற்றான் பற்றினை அப்பற்றைப்
பற்றுக பற்று விடற்கு.
transliteration:
Patruga patratraan patrinai appatraip
Patruga patru vidarku.
current_meaning: Hold on to the One who is free of all attachment. Hold on to that one bond alone, so that you can let go of all others.
elementary: When you're learning to swim, you hold on to the edge of the pool so you can stop being scared of the water. This kural says hold on to God — the one who clings to nothing — so you can let go of everything else.
university: The chapter's closing couplet repeats forms of patru (“attachment, clinging”) six times, a virtuoso climax. It resolves a paradox the chapter has built up: desire cannot simply be willed away, so Valluvar prescribes a single counter-attachment — to patratraan, 'the One without attachment', whom Parimelazhagar and most commentators identify as God, whose feet are to be held — as the instrument for dropping all other attachments. Karunanidhi, in keeping with his secular reading, takes patratraan to mean any truly detached person, making the verse a counsel to cling to the company of the detached. The strategy of replacing a lower attachment with a higher one parallels the Gita's 'higher taste', while the Buddha's raft simile adds the caution that even the means is finally to be let go.

tamil:
பொருளல்ல வற்றைப் பொருளென்று உணரும்
மருளானாம் மாணாப் பிறப்பு.
transliteration:
Porulalla vatraip porulendru unarum
Marulaanaam maanaap pirappu.
current_meaning: Thinking that things which are not real are the real thing is a mistake of the mind. From this mistake come lowly births, again and again.
elementary: Imagine chasing a shiny puddle on a hot road, sure it’s water, when it’s only a mirage. You’d run and run, get more and more thirsty, and never drink. This kural says that when we treat things that don’t last as if they were the real treasure, we keep chasing mirages again and again, life after life.
university: The chapter opens with a diagnosis rather than a prescription: the root of bondage is marul (delusion, confusion), specifically the cognitive error of taking porul-alladhu (what is not the real) for porul (the real). Commentators such as Parimelazhagar read maanaa-p-pirappu (‘inglorious birth’) as the whole cycle of transmigration, which turns the couplet into an epistemological account of samsara: rebirth is caused less by particular sins than by misperception. This closely matches the Advaita Vedanta analysis of adhyasa (superimposition, the classic rope mistaken for a snake) and the Buddhist teaching that avijja (ignorance) is the first link of dependent origination. Because the Tamil ‘porul’ is richly ambiguous (thing, wealth, meaning, reality), the couplet also carries an ethical undertone: whoever treats wealth and possessions as the ultimate ‘thing’ has mistaken the counterfeit for the coin.

tamil:
இருள்நீங்கி இன்பம் பயக்கும் மருள்நீங்கி
மாசறு காட்சி யவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Irulneengi inbam payakkum marulneengi
Maasaru kaatchi yavarkku.
current_meaning: People who have left confusion behind and see the truth clearly and without fault find that this clear sight drives away darkness and brings true joy.
elementary: When you switch on the light in a dark room, the scary shape in the corner turns out to be just a coat on a chair, and suddenly you feel safe and happy. People who see the truth clearly are like that: the light of truth chases away the darkness and fear, and joy comes in.
university: The couplet is built on a matched pair: irul neengi (darkness departs) and marul neengi (delusion departs). When inner confusion (marul) is removed, outer darkness (irul, which commentators gloss as the darkness of hell or of future births) also lifts. The key phrase maasaru kaatchi, ‘stainless seeing’, frames liberation as a kind of vision (compare the Sanskrit darshana) rather than mere intellectual agreement, and Parimelazhagar takes the resulting inbam (bliss) as the bliss of release (veedu). The light/darkness metaphor for knowledge and ignorance is shared with the Upanishads (tamaso ma jyotir gamaya), with the Buddha’s first sermon (‘illumination arose’), and with Plato’s ascent from the cave. What stands out in Valluvar is the ethical precondition built into the seeing itself: the vision must be free of stain (maasu).

tamil:
ஐயத்தின் நீங்கித் தெளிந்தார்க்கு வையத்தின்
வானம் நணிய துடைத்து.
transliteration:
Aiyaththin neengith thelindhaarkku vaiyaththin
Vaanam naniya thudaiththu.
current_meaning: For people who have moved past doubt and become truly certain, heaven is closer than the earth they stand on.
elementary: When you’re not sure which path leads home, even a short walk feels long and scary. But once you know the way for certain, home feels close. This kural says that people who have cleared away all doubt about what is true feel heaven is closer to them than the ground under their feet.
university: Aiyam (doubt) is here a technical term: Indian epistemology treats samshaya (doubt) as one of the defects of cognition that block liberation, alongside viparyaya (error), which Kural 351 addressed. Thelivu (clarity, settled understanding) is the positive term, and Valluvar’s hyperbole (vaanam naniyadhu, ‘the sky/heaven is nearer’) turns ordinary spatial logic upside down: the earth we stand on becomes the distant, precarious thing, while the spiritual goal becomes immediate. Commentators take vaanam as the higher world or liberation (veedu). The inversion echoes the Gita’s warning that the doubting soul finds happiness neither here nor hereafter, and the Mundaka Upanishad’s ‘all doubts are solved’ when the Real is seen. Comparative readers may also note Deuteronomy’s insistence that the divine word is ‘not in heaven’ but ‘very nigh unto thee’, a similar collapsing of distance, though grounded in revelation rather than insight.

tamil:
ஐயுணர்வு எய்தியக் கண்ணும் பயமின்றே
மெய்யுணர்வு இல்லா தவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Aiyunarvu eydhiyak kannum payamindre
Meyyunarvu illaa thavarkku.
current_meaning: Even if someone has fully learned everything the five senses can tell them, it is of no real use if they do not truly know what is real.
elementary: A person could have perfect eyes, sharp ears and a great nose, and still walk right past a treasure because they don’t know what it is. This kural says the five senses are like a camera: very useful, but you need a wise mind to understand what the pictures really mean.
university: Aiyunarvu, ‘five-fold awareness’, has two classical readings, both preserved in the commentary tradition. Mu. Varadarasanar and others take it as the complete knowledge gathered through the five senses, while Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar read it as the ascetic’s mastery or restraint of the five senses. Either way the claim is striking: neither sensory knowledge nor sensory discipline is enough without meyyunarvu, knowledge of the real. The second reading turns the couplet into a pointed warning to renunciants (the chapter sits in the Thuravaraviyal, the section on the ascetic life) that austerity without insight is barren. Philosophically it anticipates the argument of Plato’s Theaetetus that knowledge cannot simply be perception, and it parallels Heraclitus’s remark that eyes and ears are bad witnesses for souls that cannot interpret them.

tamil:
எப்பொருள் எத்தன்மைத் தாயினும் அப்பொருள்
மெய்ப்பொருள் காண்பது அறிவு.
transliteration:
Epporul eththanmaith thaayinum apporul
Meypporul kaanpadhu arivu.
current_meaning: Whatever a thing is, and however it looks, wisdom is seeing the real truth inside it.
elementary: Two chocolates can look exactly the same, but one might have caramel inside and the other a nut. You only know by looking inside. This kural says a wise person doesn’t stop at how things look on the outside but finds out what they really are.
university: This is the chapter’s most quoted couplet, and it works as a definition: arivu (wisdom) is meypporul kaanpadhu, ‘seeing the true thing’ in every porul, whatever its apparent nature (eththanmaith thaayinum). The chain of repetitions (epporul, apporul, meypporul) performs the act it describes, peeling ‘thing’ back to ‘true thing’. Mu. Varadarasanar’s gloss makes the point explicit: one must not be dazzled by how a thing appears but know its real nature. Modern readers often extend it to critical thinking in general, meaning not being taken in by surface, reputation, or rhetoric. The ideal is close to the Buddhist yathabhuta-ñanadassana (‘knowing and seeing things as they really are’) and to the Greek project, from Heraclitus to Plato, of distinguishing a thing’s real nature (phusis) from how it seems (doxa).

tamil:
கற்றீண்டு மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டார் தலைப்படுவர்
மற்றீண்டு வாரா நெறி.
transliteration:
Katreendu meypporul kandaar thalaippaduvar
Matreendu vaaraa neri.
current_meaning: People who have learned and have seen the True Reality here in this life set off on the path of no return, never to be born into this world again.
elementary: When you finally solve a really hard maze, you don’t have to go back into it: you’ve found the way out. This kural says that people who learn deeply and truly understand what is real find the way out of the maze of being born again and again.
university: Two emphases distinguish this couplet: kattru (having learned) and eendu (here, in this very life). Valluvar insists that realization must happen within embodied existence, a ‘liberation while living’ close to the Vedantic jivanmukti and to the Buddhist arahant who knows ‘this is the last birth’. Learning is the necessary first step, but the verb is kandaar (they saw), not merely ‘they studied’: scholarship must end in direct seeing, and Solomon Pappaiah’s gloss stresses learning from the great as the start of that process. Vaaraa neri, ‘the path of no return’, closely echoes the Gita’s ‘one who reaches it never returns’. The formula reaches across traditions: Revelation’s ‘he shall go no more out’ and the Orphic initiate’s escape from the ‘circle’ of births voice the same idea of a final exit.

tamil:
ஓர்த்துள்ளம் உள்ளது உணரின் ஒருதலையாப்
பேர்த்துள்ள வேண்டா பிறப்பு.
transliteration:
Orththullam ulladhu unarin orudhalaiyaap
Perththulla vendaa pirappu.
current_meaning: If the mind has carefully studied and firmly understood what is truly real, there is no need to think about being born again.
elementary: Once you truly understand that the monster under the bed was only a shadow, you don’t have to be scared of it again tomorrow night. This kural says that once your mind really and firmly understands what is real, you don’t have to worry about coming back to be born again.
university: Ulladhu, literally ‘that which is’, is one of the most philosophically loaded words in the chapter. It corresponds to the Sanskrit sat (Being) and later gave its name to Ramana Maharshi’s Tamil work Ulladhu Narpadhu (‘Forty Verses on That Which Is’). Orththu (having reflected or investigated) and oru-thalaiyaa (with complete, one-pointed certainty) spell out the method: truth is reached by sustained inquiry until conviction is total. Traditional glosses (Solomon Pappaiah speaks of holding fully in mind ‘what was heard from the great’) connect this to the Vedantic sequence of hearing, reflection and contemplation (shravana, manana, nididhyasana). The language of ‘what is’ invites comparison with Parmenides, for whom Being is ‘uncreated and indestructible’, and with Maimonides, for whom knowing the Primary Being is ‘the foundation of all foundations’. Valluvar’s distinctive claim is soteriological: to grasp Being is to end becoming.

tamil:
பிறப்பென்னும் பேதைமை நீங்கச் சிறப்பென்னும்
செம்பொருள் காண்பது அறிவு.
transliteration:
Pirappennum pedhaimai neengach sirappennum
Semporul kaanpadhu arivu.
current_meaning: True wisdom is seeing the perfect Truth, the Highest Good, so that the foolishness called “birth” is taken away.
elementary: Imagine being stuck on a merry-go-round that never stops because you forgot there’s an exit. The moment you notice the exit sign, you can step off. This kural says being born again and again is like forgetting the exit, and seeing what is truly real is the exit sign.
university: The couplet makes a bold equation: pirappu ennum pedhaimai, ‘the folly called birth’. Birth is not only caused by ignorance (as in 351); it is itself named a form of ignorance. Against it stands sirappu ennum semporul, ‘the perfect Truth called excellence’, which commentators read as the Supreme Being or the state of release (Mu. Varadarasanar glosses sirappu as mukti). Semporul (‘the fine, perfect substance’) is the same term used in 359 for the support of all things. Buddhism offers the closest structural parallel: in dependent origination, ignorance (avijja) is the first condition and rebirth (jati) the eleventh, so the fading of ignorance ends birth. Hindu parallels such as Gita 4.9 make knowledge of the divine the reason one ‘does not take birth again’, while John’s ‘the truth shall make you free’ expresses liberation through knowing within a linear rather than cyclical cosmology.

tamil:
சார்புணர்ந்து சார்பு கெடஒழுகின் மற்றழித்துச்
சார்தரா சார்தரு நோய்.
transliteration:
Saarbunarndhu saarbu keda ozhukin matrazhiththuch
Saardharaa saardharu noi.
current_meaning: Whoever understands what truly supports all things, and lives so that every other attachment falls away, will never be touched by the sorrows that ruin people’s efforts.
elementary: If you’re holding a hundred balloons, the wind can drag you anywhere. But if you let go of them and hold on to one strong railing, you stay safe. This kural says: know what is truly worth holding on to, let the other things go, and troubles can’t grab hold of you.
university: The couplet is built on a remarkable pun: the root saar- (‘to lean on, cling to, attach’) appears four times: saarbu unarndhu (knowing the true support), saarbu keda (so that attachments perish), saardharaa (will not cling) and saardharu noi (the afflictions that would cling). Commentators read the first saarbu as the Supreme Truth (semporul), the support of all things, and the second as worldly attachment (pattru). The wordplay thus contrasts one legitimate ‘leaning’ with many illegitimate ones. The logic, that attachment is the channel through which suffering ‘attaches’, is shared with Buddhist teaching on upadana (grasping) and with the Gita’s call to cut the world-tree ‘with the weapon of detachment’ while taking refuge in its root. Islam’s divine name as-Samad, the One on whom all depend, offers an especially close lexical parallel to the first saarbu.

tamil:
காமம் வெகுளி மயக்கம் இவ்மூன்றன்
நாமம் கெடக்கெடும் நோய்.
transliteration:
Kaamam vekuli mayakkam ivmoondran
Naamam kedakkedum noi.
current_meaning: When desire, anger and confusion are destroyed so completely that even their names are gone, the suffering they cause is destroyed too.
elementary: Weeds keep coming back if you only snip off the tops. You have to pull them out by the roots so nothing is left. This kural says greed, anger and confusion are like three weeds: pull them out so completely that even their names are forgotten, and the trouble they cause disappears.
university: The chapter closes by naming a triad: kaamam, vekuli, mayakkam (desire, anger, delusion). Its correspondence with the Buddhist ‘three roots’ or ‘three poisons’ (raga, dosa, moha: greed, hatred, delusion) is nearly exact, and it overlaps substantially with the Gita’s ‘three gates of hell’ (lust, anger, greed). Valluvar’s hyperbole, that the very names must perish (naamam keda), insists on eradication rather than suppression: not even the latent tendency or memory may remain. Because the chapter began with delusion (marul) as the cause of birth, ending with mayakkam as the third root closes the argument in a ring. True knowledge removes the delusion that fuels desire and anger, and with all three gone, the ‘disease’ (noi) of suffering and rebirth ends.

tamil:
அவாஎன்ப எல்லா உயிர்க்கும் எஞ்ஞான்றும்
தவாஅப் பிறப்பீனும் வித்து.
transliteration:
Avaa enba ellaa uyirkkum egnaandrum
Thavaaap pirappeenum viththu.
current_meaning: Wise people say that desire is the seed that, for every living being and at all times, never fails to cause one birth after another.
elementary: A seed falls into the ground and grows into a plant, and that plant drops more seeds that grow again and again. Valluvar says wanting things is like that seed: as long as we keep wanting, we keep getting planted into new lives, over and over.
university: The chapter that closes the ascetic section (Thuravaraviyal) opens by naming avaa (craving) as the vittu, the seed, of an unbroken chain of births (thavaap pirappu). The agricultural metaphor is exact: a seed holds the whole future plant, and craving holds the whole future of embodied existence, so destroying the seed leaves the cycle nothing to grow from. The word “enba” (“they say”) shows Valluvar reporting a consensus of the wise rather than inventing a doctrine, and the idea is indeed shared across Indian soteriologies: the Upanishadic teaching that desire determines rebirth, the Buddhist second noble truth that craving leads to renewed existence, and the Jain account of passions binding karma. Placed right after “Knowledge of Truth” (Meyyunarthal) and just before “Destiny” (Oozh), the chapter that ends Book 1, this chapter makes the uprooting of desire the practical summit of the renunciant’s path.

tamil:
வேண்டுங்கால் வேண்டும் பிறவாமை மற்றது
வேண்டாமை வேண்ட வரும்.
transliteration:
Vendungaal vendum piravaamai matradhu
Vendaamai venda varum.
current_meaning: If you must want something, want to be free from being born again. That freedom comes only when you want to be free of wanting.
elementary: Imagine you get just one wish. The smartest wish would be: “I wish I didn’t need any more wishes.” Valluvar says that is the one wish worth making, because it is the wish that sets you free.
university: The couplet repeats the verb vendu (“to want”) four times: vendungaal vendum … vendaamai venda. The verbal knot mirrors the paradox it describes. Valluvar admits that a person cannot simply switch off wanting, so he turns the power of desire against itself and makes piravaamai (non-birth, liberation) its one proper object. Parimelazhagar reads vendaamai as the settled state of desirelessness, so the means (wanting not to want) and the goal (not being born again) are joined. The same ‘desire for desirelessness’ paradox appears in the Buddhist distinction between wholesome aspiration (chanda) and craving (tanha), and in the Gita’s call to act without craving the fruits of action.

tamil:
வேண்டாமை அன்ன விழுச்செல்வம் ஈண்டில்லை
ஆண்டும் அஃதொப்பது இல்.
transliteration:
Vendaamai anna vizhuchchelvam eendillai
Aandum aqdhoppadhu il.
current_meaning: There is no treasure in this world as precious as being free from desire. Even in the next world, nothing is equal to it.
elementary: A kid with a giant pile of toys who always wants more still feels poor. A kid who is happy with what they have feels rich. Valluvar says not wanting is the biggest treasure there is, bigger than anything here or even in heaven.
university: Vizhuchchelvam (“choicest wealth”) turns the idea of wealth inside out: a chapter on renunciation borrows the language of ownership to describe the absence of wanting. The pair eendu (“here”) and aandu (“there”) covers both this world and the heavenly worlds that ritual religion promised as rewards. Valluvar therefore ranks desirelessness above celestial pleasures, in line with the Upanishadic and Buddhist view that heaven is only a finer object of desire. The paradox that wanting less makes one richer shows up almost word for word in Seneca, in the Hadith on ‘richness of the soul’ and in Ben Zoma’s “Who is rich?”, which makes this one of the most cross-culturally shared couplets in the chapter.

tamil:
தூஉய்மை என்பது அவாவின்மை மற்றது
வாஅய்மை வேண்ட வரும்.
transliteration:
Thoouymai enbadhu avaavinmai matradhu
Vaaaimai venda varum.
current_meaning: Being pure means nothing other than being free from desire, and that freedom comes from longing for the truth.
elementary: A glass of water looks clear when nothing is stirring it up. Your heart is “clean” when wanting isn’t stirring it. The way to keep it calm is to love what is true more than what is shiny.
university: Valluvar defines thooymai (purity) psychologically rather than ritually, not by baths, diet or caste observances but as avaavinmai, the absence of craving. The second line adds a cause: freedom from craving arises from desiring vaaymai. Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasan gloss vaaymai as meipporul, ultimate Reality, while Karunanidhi reads it as truthfulness. Either way the chapter keeps its strategy of redirecting desire, letting one longing, for truth, push out all lesser ones. The lengthened forms thoouymai and vaaaymai (alapedai, a metrical lengthening) bind the two key terms by sound as well as sense.

tamil:
அற்றவர் என்பார் அவாஅற்றார் மற்றையார்
அற்றாக அற்றது இலர்.
transliteration:
Atravar enbaar avaaatraar matraiyaar
Atraaga atradhu ilar.
current_meaning: Only people who have cut off desire truly deserve to be called people who have given up the world. Others, whatever they have given up, are not fully free like them.
elementary: Throwing your candy away doesn’t really count if you keep thinking about candy all day. Valluvar says the real “giver-upper” is the person who stopped wanting, not just the person who stopped having.
university: The couplet plays on atravar (“those who are cut off”, the renunciants) and avaa atraar (“those cut off from desire”), and ends by saying that others are not free in that full sense (atraaga atradhu ilar). Valluvar draws a sharp line between outward renunciation (robes, poverty, leaving home, the themes of the earlier chapter Thuravu) and inward renunciation. This extends his critique of the false ascetic in Chapter 28 (Koodaavozhukkam, “Imposture”). For Valluvar, freedom is measured by what one no longer wants, not by what one no longer owns.

tamil:
அஞ்சுவ தோரும் அறனே ஒருவனை
வஞ்சிப்ப தோரும் அவா.
transliteration:
Anjuva dhoorum arane oruvanai
Vanjippa dhoorum avaa.
current_meaning: Being on guard against desire is itself goodness, because it is desire that fools a person and ruins them.
elementary: Some joke toys look like candy but have a spring inside that jumps out at you, so you learn to be careful of them. Valluvar says wanting things is a trick like that. It fools us, so being careful of it is part of being good.
university: The couplet frames the ethical life as vigilance: aran (virtue) here simply is the fearing (anjuvadhu) of avaa, because avaa is what vanjippadhu, what cheats and betrays a person. Commentators such as Mu. Varadarasan add that desire waits for a moment of weakness (sorvu) to strike, much as a thief waits for the watchman to nod off. The repeated expletive oorum gives the line a proverbial, almost incantatory rhythm. This picture of desire as a cunning inner enemy parallels the Gita’s portrait of kama as an “all-devouring” foe and the biblical image of sin crouching at the door.

tamil:
அவாவினை ஆற்ற அறுப்பின் தவாவினை
தான்வேண்டு மாற்றான் வரும்.
transliteration:
Avaavinai aatra aruppin thavaavinai
Thaan vendum aatraan varum.
current_meaning: If a person cuts off desire completely, the good deeds that lead to a life free from death will come to them just as they wish.
elementary: When you stop grabbing at every toy in the store, your hands are finally free to hold what really matters. Valluvar says that when you drop all your wants, good deeds that last forever come to you easily.
university: Aatra aruppin, “if one cuts utterly”, insists on total rather than partial removal and echoes the chapter title’s aruththal (“cutting”). Thavaa vinai, “unfailing” or “imperishable action”, is glossed by commentators as the deeds that bring deathlessness, that is, liberation. The promise that these deeds arrive thaan vendum aatraan (“in the way he wishes”) holds a quiet irony: the person who has stopped wanting finally gets what he wants. The same paradox, that giving up self-will lines the will up with the good, appears in Stoic acceptance of fate, in the rabbinic “do His will as though it were your will”, and in the Katha Upanishad’s promise that the desireless mortal becomes immortal.

tamil:
அவாஇல்லார்க் கில்லாகுந் துன்பம் அஃதுண்டேல்
தவாஅது மேன்மேல் வரும்.
transliteration:
Avaa illaarkku illaagum thunbam aqdhundel
Thavaaadhu menmel varum.
current_meaning: People without desire have no sorrow. Wherever desire exists, sorrow keeps coming, one after another, without fail.
elementary: Every time you want something you can’t have, you feel a little sad. If you want a hundred things, you get a hundred little sads. Want nothing, and the sads have nowhere to come from.
university: The couplet is a strict pair of conditions. For those without desire (avaa illaarkku), suffering ceases to exist (illaagum); if desire exists (aqdhundel), suffering comes thavaaadhu menmel, without fail, one upon another. The doubled menmel (“more and more, upon and upon”) imitates the way craving compounds, since each satisfied desire breeds new ones. This is the Kural’s closest approach to a formal statement of the Buddhist second noble truth, but Valluvar stays practical rather than metaphysical: he describes the lived economy of wanting, not a theory of dependent origination.

tamil:
இன்பம் இடையறா தீண்டும் அவாவென்னும்
துன்பத்துள் துன்பங் கெடின்.
transliteration:
Inbam idaiyaraa theendum avaavennum
Thunbaththul thunbam kedin.
current_meaning: When desire, the worst of all sorrows, is destroyed, joy flows without stopping, even in this life.
elementary: Imagine an itch you’ve had for so long that you forgot it was there. When it finally stops, you feel wonderful all the time. Valluvar says wanting is that itch, and when it’s gone, happiness just keeps going.
university: Valluvar calls avaa “thunbaththul thunbam”, the sorrow among sorrows, the one that gives rise to all the others. Removing it therefore does more than take away one pain: it dries up the source of every pain. The promised result, inbam idaiyaraadhu eendum, is unbroken joy “even here” (eendum), a this-worldly liberation comparable to the Upanishadic jivanmukta and to the Buddhist realization of nibbana in this very life. The joy is defined negatively, as what remains when craving stops. That lines up closely with the Buddhist third noble truth and with Epicurus’s definition of pleasure as freedom from disturbance.

tamil:
ஆரா இயற்கை அவாநீப்பின் அந்நிலையே
பேரா இயற்கை தரும்.
transliteration:
Aaraa iyarkai avaa neeppin annilaiye
Peraa iyarkai tharum.
current_meaning: Desire by its nature can never be satisfied. Whoever throws it away gains, at that very moment, a lasting happiness that never changes.
elementary: Trying to fill a bucket that has a hole in the bottom never works. You pour and pour, and it’s never full. Valluvar says wanting is that leaky bucket. Stop pouring into it, and you find a calm that never runs out.
university: The final couplet crowns the chapter with a mirrored wordplay: aaraa iyarkai (a nature that is never filled) against peraa iyarkai (a nature that never departs). Insatiability is what defines desire, and permanence is the reward for giving it up, the unchanging state that commentators identify with liberation (veedu). The word annilaiye (“in that very state” or “at that very moment”) suggests the reward is not postponed to some later heaven but is the same thing as the act of letting go. As the last couplet on renunciation before the chapter on Destiny that closes the Book of Virtue, it sums up Valluvar’s whole ascetic path: the endlessly hungry becomes the endlessly at peace.

tamil:
ஆகூழால் தோன்றும் அசைவின்மை கைப்பொருள்
போகூழால் தோன்றும் மடி.
transliteration:
Aakoozhaal thondrum asaivinmai kaipporul
Pokoozhaal thondrum madi.
current_meaning: When fate is ready to bring you riches, it makes you work hard without tiring. When fate is ready to take riches away, it makes you lazy.
elementary: Imagine two kids with the same homework. One suddenly feels full of energy and finishes it; the other feels sleepy and gives up. This kural says that even the energy or the sleepiness you feel can be part of your fate: good fortune shows up as hard work, and bad fortune shows up as laziness.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter with a subtle psychological claim: fate (ஊழ், uzh) does not merely deliver outcomes from outside but works through the agent’s own dispositions. ஆகூழ் (aakuzh, ‘fate of gaining’) manifests as அசைவின்மை (unflagging perseverance), while போகூழ் (pokuzh, ‘fate of losing’) manifests as மடி (sloth). This neatly reconciles the chapter with the Kural’s many praises of effort elsewhere (e.g. the later chapters on ஆள்வினையுடைமை): effort is praised, yet the very capacity to make effort is itself read as a sign of a favourable destiny. Commentators such as Parimelazhagar treat ஊழ் as the ripened fruit of past deeds (பழவினை), which makes the idea closer to karmic causation than to arbitrary luck. The structure anticipates the Stoic ‘co-fated’ reply to the Lazy Argument: outcome and effort are fated together, so fatalism is no excuse for idleness.

tamil:
பேதைப் படுக்கும் இழவூழ் அறிவகற்றும்
ஆகலூழ் உற்றக் கடை.
transliteration:
Pedhaip padukkum izhavoozh arivagatrum
Aagaloozh utrak kadai.
current_meaning: When fate brings loss, it makes even a clever person act foolishly. When fate brings gain, it opens up a person’s mind and makes it wider.
elementary: Have you ever had a day when you kept making silly mistakes, and another day when every answer just clicked? This kural says bad fortune can make even smart people act silly, and good fortune can make people seem wiser than usual.
university: The couplet extends the previous one from will to intellect: இழவூழ் (izhavuzh, ‘the fate of loss’) makes one பேதை (a fool), while ஆகலூழ் (aagaluzh, ‘the fate of increase’) அறிவு அகற்றும், widening or enlarging understanding. Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasan read அகற்றும் as ‘to expand’, not ‘to remove’. The idea is that judgement itself is vulnerable to fortune: brilliant people make ruinous decisions when their luck is turning. The same intuition appears across cultures as the sense that those heading for ruin are first robbed of good judgement, and in the biblical account of Ahithophel’s wise counsel being ‘defeated’ by divine design. Philosophically, it raises the question of moral luck: how far our rationality depends on circumstances we do not control.

tamil:
நுண்ணிய நூல்பல கற்பினும் மற்றுந்தன்
உண்மை யறிவே மிகும்.
transliteration:
Nunniya noolpala karpinum matrundhan
Unmai yarive migum.
current_meaning: However many deep books a person studies, in the end the understanding that fate has given them is what wins out.
elementary: You can give a pencil to every child in class, but each one will still draw in their own way. This kural says that reading many clever books helps, but in the end a person’s own natural understanding decides how they really think and act.
university: The key phrase is உண்மை அறிவு (unmai arivu): literally ‘the knowledge that truly is’ one’s own, which commentators gloss as the understanding given by ஊழ், as opposed to what is acquired from books (நூல்). Valluvar is not dismissing learning; he devotes whole chapters to கல்வி (learning). He is noting that learning is filtered through an innate capacity it cannot fully override. The Gita makes a parallel claim that even the learned act according to their own nature (prakṛti), and Heraclitus’ fragment that character is a person’s daimon points the same way. Modern debates on nature versus nurture, and on the limits of education, are a secular version of the same observation.

tamil:
இருவேறு உலகத்து இயற்கை திருவேறு
தெள்ளிய ராதலும் வேறு.
transliteration:
Iruveru ulagaththu iyarkai thiruveru
Thelliya raadhalum veru.
current_meaning: Fate works in two different ways in the world. Becoming rich is one thing, and becoming wise is quite another.
elementary: Some kids are great at sports and others are great at math, and being good at one doesn’t make you good at the other. This kural says money and wisdom work the same way: being rich and being wise come from different kinds of luck, so one doesn’t guarantee the other.
university: The couplet makes an observation anyone can check: wealth (திரு, thiru, also the name of the goddess of fortune) and clear wisdom (தெள்ளியர் ஆதல்) are handed out on separate tracks. The rich are often not wise, and the wise are often not rich. Commentators read இருவேறு இயற்கை as two distinct operations of ஊழ். Indian folk tradition expresses the same idea as the old rivalry between Lakshmi (wealth) and Saraswati (learning). Ecclesiastes’ remark that bread is not always to the wise nor riches to the understanding, the Talmudic teaching on sustenance depending on mazal rather than merit, and Aristotle’s puzzle about fortunate fools all record the same gap between intelligence and worldly reward.

tamil:
நல்லவை எல்லாஅந் தீயவாம் தீயவும்
நல்லவாம் செல்வம் செயற்கு.
transliteration:
Nallavai ellaaan theeyavaam theeyavum
Nallavaam selvam seyarku.
current_meaning: When you are trying to get rich, fate can turn every good chance into a bad one, and every bad chance into a good one.
elementary: Sometimes you plan a picnic on a sunny day and it rains anyway. Other times you get stuck indoors and end up finding something wonderful. This kural says that when it comes to making money, luck can flip good chances into bad ones and bad chances into good ones.
university: Commentators take நல்லவை and தீயவை here as circumstances favourable or unfavourable to earning, such as the right time, place, means and partners, rather than moral good and evil. Solomon Pappaiah glosses the kural this way: even with the right time, place and trade, an adverse fate brings loss, and even without them a favourable fate brings profit. The couplet warns against over-confidence in planning, since the same conditions can produce opposite results depending on forces beyond calculation. Across traditions this becomes the theme of reversal: the Qur'an’s ‘perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you’, Rabbi Akiva’s night journey, and Boethius’ turning wheel of Fortune.

tamil:
பரியினும் ஆகாவாம் பாலல்ல உய்த்துச்
சொரியினும் போகா தம.
transliteration:
Pariyinum aagaavaam paalalla uyththuch
Choriyinum pogaa thama.
current_meaning: What fate has not made yours will not stay, however carefully you guard it. What fate has made yours will not leave, even if you throw it away.
elementary: Imagine holding sand tightly in your fist: it still slips out. Now imagine a boomerang: you throw it away and it comes back. This kural says things that aren’t meant for you slip away however hard you hold on, and things that are meant for you come back even if you throw them away.
university: The couplet turns on பால் (paal), ‘share’ or ‘portion’, the same word used for the three books of the Kural. Things outside one’s allotted share (பாலல்ல) cannot be kept even with painful guarding (பரியினும்), and things within it (தம) will not leave even if deliberately poured out (உய்த்துச் சொரியினும்). It is an extreme statement of possession as destiny. Greek tradition gives a near-perfect illustration in Polycrates’ ring, which was thrown into the sea and came back inside a fish. The ethical point, drawn out by Stoics like Epictetus, is that anxious clinging is irrational: one should hold possessions loosely, as things on loan.

tamil:
வகுத்தான் வகுத்த வகையல்லால் கோடி
தொகுத்தார்க்கு துய்த்தல் அரிது.
transliteration:
Vaguththaan vaguththa vagaiyallaal kodi
Thoguththaarkku thuyththal aridhu.
current_meaning: Even people who pile up crores (tens of millions) of money can enjoy it only as much as the One who decides fate allows. Beyond that, they cannot enjoy it.
elementary: You could fill a whole room with candy, but if you have a toothache you can’t eat any of it. This kural says that piling up huge amounts of money doesn’t mean you’ll get to enjoy it; how much you actually enjoy is decided by fate.
university: The striking phrase வகுத்தான் வகுத்த வகை (‘the way apportioned by the Apportioner’) is one of the few places where Valluvar speaks of fate through an agent. Commentators differ on whether வகுத்தான் means God or the impersonal law of past deeds. The kural separates possession from enjoyment (துய்த்தல்): accumulation is within human reach, but the capacity to enjoy is allotted. The same gap appears in Ecclesiastes’ rich man to whom God does not give ‘power to eat thereof’, in Jesus’ parable of the rich fool, and in the myth of Midas starving amid gold. This makes the couplet a critique of hoarding as well as a statement about fate.

tamil:
துறப்பார்மன் துப்புர வில்லார் உறற்பால
ஊட்டா கழியு மெனின்.
transliteration:
Thurappaarman thuppura villaar urarpaala
Oottaa kazhiyu menin.
current_meaning: Poor people, who have nothing to enjoy, would give up the world, if only fate let the sufferings meant for them pass by without making them go through them.
elementary: Imagine someone with an empty lunchbox. You might think it would be easy for them to say ‘I don’t need lunch.’ But they still feel hungry. This kural says poor people would give up wanting things and become monks, but fate still makes them feel the troubles they are meant to go through, so they can’t let go.
university: This is the chapter’s most compressed and most debated couplet. துப்புரவு (thuppuravu) means the means of enjoyment; those without it (the destitute) would seem to be natural renunciants, since they have nothing to give up. The particle மன் signals an unrealised possibility: they *would* renounce, *if* the sufferings that are theirs to experience (உறற்பால) passed away without being fed to them (ஊட்டா கழியும்). The implication is ironic: poverty does not automatically produce detachment, because fate still insists that its allotted pains be tasted. This fits the karmic principle, shared with Buddhism and Jainism, that ripened deeds must be experienced and cannot simply be skipped.

tamil:
நன்றாங்கால் நல்லவாக் காண்பவர் அன்றாங்கால்
அல்லற் படுவ தெவன்.
transliteration:
Nandraangaal nallavaak kaanbavar andraangaal
Allar paduva thevan.
current_meaning: People who happily accept good times as good, why should they get upset when bad times come? Both come from the same fate.
elementary: When you win a game you say ‘Yay, lucky me!’ So when you lose, why get so upset? Both winning and losing come from the same luck. This kural asks us to take the bad days as calmly as we enjoy the good ones.
university: The couplet is a rhetorical question with a Stoic edge. If good fortune (நன்று) and misfortune (அன்று) both come from ஊழ், then welcoming one and lamenting the other is inconsistent. Mu. Varadarasan glosses it as good deeds and evil deeds ripening, which ties the couplet to karmic reasoning. The ethical advice is equanimity (சமநிலை): accept both outcomes as coming from one source. It is closely echoed in Job’s reply to his wife, in the Mishnah’s rule to bless God for the bad as for the good, in the Gita’s teaching on bearing pleasure and pain alike, in the Buddha’s eight worldly conditions, and in Nietzsche’s amor fati.

tamil:
ஊழிற் பெருவலி யாவுள மற்றொன்று
சூழினுந் தான்முந் துறும்.
transliteration:
Oozhir peruvali yaavula matrondru
Soozhinun thaanmun thurum.
current_meaning: What is stronger than fate? Even when a person finds another way to escape it, fate gets there first.
elementary: Imagine playing tag with someone who always knows which way you’ll run and is already waiting there. That’s how this kural describes fate: whatever clever path you choose to avoid it, fate is already there ahead of you.
university: The chapter, and with it the whole Book of Virtue (அறத்துப்பால்), ends on a rhetorical question: ஊழிற் பெருவலி யாவுள, ‘what is of greater strength than fate?’ The second line gives the reason: even if one plans (சூழினும்) another course, fate itself arrives first (தான் முந்துறும்). The positioning matters. After thirty-seven chapters on virtue, Valluvar closes by acknowledging the limits of human agency. Book 2 (Porul) then opens with vigorous chapters on effort, and later ones such as ஆள்வினையுடைமை (e.g. Kural 620) even assert that tireless striving can push fate aside. The tension is intended, and it mirrors the Stoic formula that fate leads the willing and drags the unwilling, as well as the Oedipus myth, in which the flight from prophecy is what fulfils it.

tamil:
படைகுடி கூழ்அமைச்சு நட்பரண் ஆறும்
உடையான் அரசருள் ஏறு.
transliteration:
Padai kudi koozh amaichu natparan aarum
Udaiyaan arasarul eru.
current_meaning: A ruler who has all six parts of a strong country (an army, loyal people, riches, wise advisers, friendly allies and strong forts) is like a lion among kings.
elementary: Think of a strong table that needs all its legs to stand. A kingdom needs six “legs”: soldiers, happy people, food and money, good helpers, friends, and strong walls. A king who has all six is like the lion — the strongest of all the kings.
university: Valluvar opens the Book of Polity not with the king’s personality but with a structural inventory of the state: padai (army), kudi (citizenry), koozh (food/revenue), amaichu (ministry), natpu (alliances), and aran (fortification). This six-limbed model closely parallels the saptanga (“seven-limbed”) theory of the state found in Kautilya’s Arthashastra, minus the king himself — who in the Kural is the one who ‘possesses’ the six, making him the integrating seventh element. The image of the ‘eru’ (a male lion or bull, the pre-eminent male of its kind) frames kingship as excellence in a competitive field of rulers rather than divine right. The chapter structure of the Porutpaal then follows this list, with later chapters devoted to each limb (army, fortress, friendship, ministers), so this kural functions as a table of contents for the whole book of statecraft.

tamil:
அஞ்சாமை ஈகை அறிவூக்கம் இந்நான்கும்
எஞ்சாமை வேந்தர்க் கியல்பு.
transliteration:
Anjaamai eegai arivookkam innaankum
Enjaamai vendhark kiyalbu.
current_meaning: Courage, generosity, wisdom and energy: never lacking these four is the true nature of a king.
elementary: A good team captain is brave, shares with everyone, knows what to do, and never gets lazy. This kural says a real king must have all four of these — and never run out of any of them.
university: Having described the external assets of the state, Valluvar now names the four inner qualities of the ruler: anjaamai (fearlessness), eegai (liberality), arivu (wisdom), and ookkam (energy or zeal). The key word is enjaamai — ‘without deficiency’ — which makes the standard one of constancy: a king who is brave in one crisis but timid in the next, or generous only when convenient, does not meet it. Commentators such as Parimelazhagar pair the qualities functionally: courage and energy to act, wisdom to decide rightly, and generosity to bind people to the ruler. The list resembles the Bhagavad Gita’s catalogue of kshatriya traits and Plato’s requirements for the philosopher-ruler, suggesting a widely shared intuition that rulership needs both a warrior’s nerve and a sage’s judgment.

tamil:
தூங்காமை கல்வி துணிவுடைமை இம்மூன்றும்
நீங்கா நிலனான் பவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Thoongaamai kalvi thunivudaimai immoondrum
Neengaa nilanaan bavarkku.
current_meaning: Being alert and never slow, being learned, and being brave and firm: these three must never leave those who rule a land.
elementary: A good lifeguard never falls asleep on duty, knows how to swim and rescue, and jumps in bravely when needed. A ruler needs the same three things: stay awake, keep learning, and be brave enough to act.
university: Thoongaamai literally means ‘not sleeping’, and the commentators read it as freedom from sloth and delay — prompt action when action is due. Kalvi (learning) and thunivu (decisive courage) complete the triad, and the verb neengaa (‘must not depart’) again stresses that these are permanent dispositions, not occasional performances. The combination is significant: learning without resolve produces a hesitant ruler, and resolve without learning produces a reckless one, while both fail without vigilance. Kautilya’s Arthashastra makes the same point in its timetable for the king, which divides the day and night into tasks and insists that the king ‘shall ever be wakeful’.

tamil:
அறனிழுக்கா தல்லவை நீக்கி மறனிழுக்கா
மானம் உடைய தரசு.
transliteration:
Aranizhukkaa thallavai neekki maranizhukkaa
Maanam udaiya tharasu.
current_meaning: A true king never turns away from what is right, removes what is wrong from the land, and keeps a brave sense of honor that never falls short.
elementary: A good referee always follows the rules, sends off players who cheat, and is brave enough to make hard calls. This kural says a real ruler is like that: always fair, stops wrongdoing, and never loses courage or self-respect.
university: The couplet is built on a pair of parallel negatives: aran izhukkaa (not slipping from dharma) and maran izhukkaa (not slipping from martial valour), bound together by maanam — honour or self-respect. Between them sits the positive duty allavai neekki, ‘removing what is not right’, which commentators read both as the king avoiding vice himself and as his suppressing wrongdoing in the realm. The effect is to insist that courage and justice must travel together: valour without righteousness becomes tyranny, while righteousness without valour cannot protect anyone. This coupling of justice and courage has a close analogue in Cicero’s claim that greatness of spirit divorced from justice is a vice rather than a virtue.

tamil:
இயற்றலும் ஈட்டலுங் காத்தலும் காத்த
வகுத்தலும் வல்ல தரசு.
transliteration:
Iyatralum eettalung kaaththalum kaaththa
Vaguththalum valla tharasu.
current_meaning: A good ruler knows how to create sources of money, collect it, keep it safe, and then share out what was kept safe in a wise way.
elementary: Think of a farmer who plants seeds, harvests the crop, stores it safely in a barn, and then shares it out so everyone has food all year. A good ruler does the same with the country’s wealth: make it, collect it, protect it, and share it fairly.
university: This is the Kural’s compact theory of public finance, expressed as four verbs: iyatral (generating new sources of revenue), eettal (collecting), kaaththal (guarding), and vaguththal (apportioning or allocating). The sequence is cyclical — well-allocated spending produces the prosperity from which new revenue is generated — and it treats wealth as a means of governance rather than a royal possession. Commentators note that vaguththal implies planned allocation among competing ends (defence, welfare, religious and civic works), not merely generosity. The same logic appears in Kalidasa’s praise of King Dilipa, who taxed his people only as the sun draws up water, in order to return it a thousandfold as rain.

tamil:
காட்சிக் கெளியன் கடுஞ்சொல்லன் அல்லனேல்
மீக்கூறும் மன்னன் நிலம்.
transliteration:
Kaatchik keliyan kadunjollan allanel
Meekkoorum mannan nilam.
current_meaning: If a king is easy for his people to meet and never speaks harshly, the whole world will praise his land.
elementary: Imagine a school principal whose door is always open and who speaks kindly to every student. Everyone would say that’s a great school! A king who is easy to meet and never speaks rudely makes his whole country admired.
university: Kaatchikku eliyan — ‘easy to be seen’ — names the political virtue of accessibility: a ruler who can be reached by ordinary petitioners without layers of gatekeepers. The second condition, not being kadunjollan (a speaker of harsh words), concerns the manner of the encounter once access is granted. The reward is striking: it is the land (nilam), not merely the king, that the world exalts, implying that a ruler’s approachability shapes the reputation of the whole polity. Kautilya warns in almost identical terms that a king who makes himself inaccessible breeds confusion and public disaffection, and Islamic tradition records a hadith threatening divine seclusion from the ruler who secludes himself from his people.

tamil:
இன்சொலால் ஈத்தளிக்க வல்லார்க்குத் தன்சொலால்
தான்கண் டனைத்திவ் வுலகு.
transliteration:
Insolaal eeththalikka vallaarkkuth thansolaal
Thaankan danaiththiv vulagu.
current_meaning: For a ruler who gives with kind words and protects the people, the world will praise him and follow his word, just as he wishes.
elementary: When a friend shares their snacks and says something nice while doing it, everyone wants to be on their team. A king who gives generously, speaks kindly, and protects people finds that the whole world is happy to follow him.
university: The kural joins three verbs — speaking sweetly (insol), giving (eeththal), and protecting (alittal) — and makes their combination the source of consent. The second line is compressed: ‘the world becomes as he sees it by his word’, which commentators such as Parimelazhagar read as the world both praising him and conforming to his intentions. The insight is that legitimacy is earned through the manner as well as the substance of benefaction: gifts given with contempt create resentment, whereas gifts with kind words create loyalty. This closely matches the Buddhist ‘bases of fellowship’ (generosity, kind speech, beneficial help, consistency) and the counsel Rehoboam’s elders gave him — ‘speak good words to them, then they will be thy servants for ever’.

tamil:
முறைசெய்து காப்பாற்றும் மன்னவன் மக்கட்கு
இறையென்று வைக்கப் படும்.
transliteration:
Muraiseydhu kaappaatrum mannavan makkatku
Iraiyendru vaikkap padum.
current_meaning: A king who rules fairly and protects his people will be seen by them as a god.
elementary: When a lifeguard keeps everyone safe and is always fair, the swimmers look up to them like a hero. This kural says a ruler who is fair and protects everyone is looked up to by the people almost like God.
university: The word irai carries a deliberate double meaning — both ‘lord/king’ and ‘God’ — and the chapter title Iraimaatchi itself plays on it. Crucially, Valluvar makes divinity conditional: the king is ‘placed’ (vaikkappadum) as god by the people only because he does murai (justice, due order) and protects them. This inverts the claim of inherent divine kingship found in texts like the Laws of Manu, grounding sacral status in performance rather than birth. Aristotle’s remark that a person of pre-eminent virtue ‘may truly be deemed a God among men’ and Psalm 82’s address to judges as ‘gods’ who must defend the poor show the same conditional logic.

tamil:
செவிகைப்பச் சொற்பொறுக்கும் பண்புடை வேந்தன்
கவிகைக்கீழ்த் தங்கும் உலகு.
transliteration:
Sevikaippach sorporukkum panbudai vendhan
Kavigaikkeezhth thangum ulagu.
current_meaning: The whole world will live safely under the royal umbrella (the sign of his rule) of a king who is kind enough to listen to words that are bitter to hear.
elementary: Good medicine often tastes bad, but it makes you better. A wise king listens even when someone tells him an unpleasant truth. Because of that, everyone feels safe living under his rule.
university: Sevi kaippa — ‘so that the ear tastes bitterness’ — is a vivid synaesthetic image for criticism that is unpleasant to hear. The commentators specify that these are the admonitions of wise elders and ministers, whose duty (developed in the later chapter on ‘Seeking the Help of the Great’) is to rebuke the king when needed. The kavigai (royal parasol) is the symbol of sovereign protection, so the kural’s claim is that tolerance of criticism is not a weakness but the condition under which the whole world will rest securely under the ruler’s shade. Vidura’s warning in the Mahabharata that speakers and hearers of unpleasant but healing words are rare, and Marcus Aurelius’ readiness to be corrected, express the same insight.

tamil:
கொடையளி செங்கோல் குடியோம்பல் நான்கும்
உடையானாம் வேந்தர்க் கொளி.
transliteration:
Kodaiyali sengol kudiyombal naangum
Udaiyaanaam vendhark koli.
current_meaning: A king who has these four things, generosity, kindness, fair rule and care for his people, is the light among kings.
elementary: In a dark room, a lamp helps everyone see. This kural says the best king is like a lamp for all other kings, because he gives generously, is kind, rules fairly, and takes care of his people.
university: The chapter closes with a second set of four, this time outward-facing: kodai (gifts), ali (grace or compassion), sengol (the ‘straight sceptre’, i.e., just rule), and kudi ombal (nurturing the people). Where 382 described the king’s inner capacities, this kural describes their effects on subjects, and it crowns the one who has them as oli — the lamp or radiance — of kings, a model by which other rulers are measured. The sengol (straight sceptre) is a central symbol of Tamil political thought, contrasted with the kodungol (crooked sceptre) of the tyrant in later chapters. The image of the just ruler as light recurs in David’s last words in 2 Samuel, and the Hebrew Bible’s ‘sceptre of righteousness’ offers a remarkably close verbal parallel.

tamil:
கற்க கசடறக் கற்பவை கற்றபின்
நிற்க அதற்குத் தக.
transliteration:
Karka kasadarak karpavai katrapin
Nirka adharkuth thaga.
current_meaning: Learn what is worth learning, and learn it fully, without gaps. Then live in a way that matches what you have learned.
elementary: Imagine learning all the rules of football perfectly but then cheating in the game. That would make the learning pointless. This kural says two things: learn good things properly, then actually live by them.
university: The chapter on Kalvi opens with a two-step command. The first is கற்க கசடற: learn so that no flaw (kasadu) is left, which traditional commentators such as Parimelazhagar read as choosing the right texts and also removing one's own mental faults through study. The second is நிற்க அதற்குத் தக: stand, or remain, in conduct fitting to that learning. The verb நிற்க (to stand) is significant, because it pictures learning as a place one lives in and not only a set of facts one holds. Because the chapter sits in the Porul section, just after the chapter on kingship, this is also advice to rulers: a king's learning is shown in how he governs, not in how much he can recite. The same link between knowing and doing appears across many traditions, from the Epistle of James to the Stoic Epictetus.

tamil:
எண்ணென்ப ஏனை எழுத்தென்ப இவ்விரண்டும்
கண்ணென்ப வாழும் உயிர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Ennenba enai ezhuthenba ivvirandum
Kannenba vaazhum uyirkku.
current_meaning: What we call numbers and what we call letters, wise people say, are the two eyes of every living person.
elementary: You have two eyes to see the world. Valluvar says your mind also has two eyes: numbers and letters. Maths and reading let you understand things you could never see without them.
university: This kural reduces the whole of learning to two basic disciplines, எண் (en, number and calculation) and எழுத்து (ezhuthu, letters and literacy), and calls them the two eyes of human life. Commentators widened the terms. Parimelazhagar took en to cover arithmetic and the sciences such as astronomy, and ezhuthu to cover grammar and literature. The modern commentator Solomon Pappaiah even glosses them as science and the arts. The repeated என்ப ('they say') presents this as settled wisdom, not personal opinion. The image of eyes prepares for the next kural, where lacking learning is compared to having sores instead of eyes. Remarkably, Aeschylus' Prometheus names the very same pair, numbers and the combining of letters, as the founding gifts of civilization.

tamil:
கண்ணுடையர் என்பவர் கற்றோர் முகத்திரண்டு
புண்ணுடையர் கல்லா தவர்.
transliteration:
Kannudaiyar enbavar katror mugaththirandu
Punnudaiyar kallaa thavar.
current_meaning: Only educated people can truly be said to have eyes. People without learning just have two sores on their face.
elementary: Two holes in your face are not the same as seeing. If you never learn anything, your eyes look at the world but understand nothing. Valluvar says a person who learns has real eyes.
university: Continuing the eye metaphor of Kural 392, Valluvar reaches one of the harshest images in the chapter. The unlearned person's eyes are புண் (pun), wounds or sores: openings in the face that do nothing and may even be painful.
