The contrast rests on the difference between physical sight and understanding. Kalaignar's commentary draws the corollary that a learned person without physical sight still 'has eyes', while an unlearned person with sight does not. The rhetoric is deliberately provocative. It belongs to a statecraft section meant to push kings and citizens toward education, and the following chapter, Kallaamai (Ignorance), develops the same harshness. Similar contrasts between seeing eyes and a seeing mind run through the Gospels, the Qur'an and Plato.

tamil:
உவப்பத் தலைக்கூடி உள்ளப் பிரிதல்
அனைத்தே புலவர் தொழில்.
transliteration:
Uvappath thalaikkoodi ullap piridhal
Anaiththe pulavar thozhil.
current_meaning: This is the sign of learned people: others are happy to meet them, and when they leave, others keep thinking of them and want to meet them again.
elementary: Think of a teacher or grandparent whose stories you love. When they come, you are happy. When they leave, you wish they could stay longer. Valluvar says that is how learned people make everyone feel.
university: Here Valluvar moves from the value of learning to its social effect. The புலவர் (pulavar, the learned or poet-scholar) is defined by an experience they create in others: உவப்ப, gladness at meeting, and உள்ளப் பிரிதல், parting in a way that leaves people thinking of them. The word தொழில் (thozhil, occupation or characteristic work) suggests that bringing joy through conversation is the scholar's real 'profession'. Commentators such as Mu. Varadarasan gloss the second half as others wondering when they will see such a person again. The kural implicitly contrasts true learning, which is generous and delightful, with pedantry that makes people glad to leave. Greek tradition offers vivid parallels, from Odysseus spellbinding the Phaeacians to Alcibiades' account of being enchanted by Socrates' words.

tamil:
உடையார்முன் இல்லார்போல் ஏக்கற்றுங் கற்றார்
கடையரே கல்லா தவர்.
transliteration:
Udaiyaarmun illaarpol ekkatrum katraar
Kadaiyare kallaa thavar.
current_meaning: People who stand respectfully before their teachers, as eager as the poor before the rich, and so gain learning, are truly great. Those who will not do this to learn are the lowest of all.
elementary: A hungry child waits eagerly for food. A good student waits just as eagerly to learn from a teacher, and is not too proud to ask. The kural says being too proud to learn is what really makes you low.
university: The kural draws on a social image any reader would recognize: the needy person standing anxiously (ஏக்கற்று) before the wealthy. It applies that image to the student before the teacher. What looks like humiliation is really the road to greatness, since those who learn this way are the truly elevated (கற்றார்), while those who refuse to learn are கடையர், the lowest. Solomon Pappaiah reads the second line as condemning those who are ashamed to stand and learn, which makes pride the real barrier to education. The inversion of rank is typical of Valluvar: outward humility produces inner eminence. Many traditions make the same point, from the Gita's call to approach a teacher with submission (echoed in the Sanskrit maxim vidyā dadāti vinayam, 'learning gives humility') to the Mishnah's warning that the shy or ashamed cannot learn.

tamil:
தொட்டனைத் தூறும் மணற்கேணி மாந்தர்க்குக்
கற்றனைத் தூறும் அறிவு.
transliteration:
Thottanaith thoorum manarkeni maandharkkuk
Katranaith thoorum arivu.
current_meaning: A well dug in sand gives more water the deeper it is dug. In the same way, a person’s understanding grows the more they learn.
elementary: When you dig a hole at the beach, water starts to seep in, and the deeper you dig, the more water comes. Your mind works the same way: the more you learn, the more wisdom flows out of you.
university: This is perhaps the most quoted kural of the chapter. It rests on a precise agricultural image from the Tamil landscape: the மணற்கேணி, a shallow well dug in sandy riverbed or soil, where groundwater seeps in more strongly the deeper one digs. The parallel verbs தொட்டனை ('as much as dug') and கற்றனை ('as much as learned') set up an exact proportion, and the shared verb ஊறும் ('springs, oozes up') links the two halves. The point is that wisdom (அறிவு, arivu) is not poured in from outside but springs up from within, released by the labour of study. It also implies that learning has no fixed end, since there is always more water below. Parallels range from Proverbs' 'wellspring of wisdom' and the Mishnah's 'ever-flowing spring' to Pope's 'Pierian spring'.

tamil:
யாதானும் நாடாமால் ஊராமால் என்னொருவன்
சாந்துணையுங் கல்லாத வாறு.
transliteration:
Yaadhaanum naadaamaal ooraamaal ennoruvan
Saanthunaiyum kallaadha vaaru.
current_meaning: For a learned person, every country and every town becomes their own. So why does anyone stay without learning right up to the day they die?
elementary: A good doctor or teacher can move to any town and still be welcomed and needed. What you learn goes with you everywhere and makes you at home anywhere. So why would anyone ever stop learning?
university: The kural is built as a rhetorical question. Its premise is that for the learned, யாதானும் நாடாம், ஊராம் (any land is their land, any town is their town), because learning makes a person welcome and useful anywhere. Its conclusion asks why anyone would remain unlearned சாந்துணையும், 'even until death'. That phrase quietly adds the idea of lifelong learning: there is no age at which study becomes pointless. In the Porul section's concern with the practical world, this is an argument from utility. Land and local status can be lost, but learning is portable citizenship. The first idea matches the Sanskrit maxim that a scholar is honoured everywhere, and the second matches Solon's line about growing old while always learning.

tamil:
ஒருமைக்கண் தான்கற்ற கல்வி ஒருவற்கு
எழுமையும் ஏமாப் புடைத்து.
transliteration:
Orumaikkan thaankatra kalvi oruvarku
Ezhumaiyum emaap pudaiththu.
current_meaning: The learning a person gains in one life can protect and help them for seven lives to come.
elementary: Planting a tree helps you, your children and your grandchildren long after you have gone. Valluvar says learning is even bigger than that: what you learn now keeps helping you far into the future, even into future lives.
university: This kural draws on the Indian framework of rebirth. ஒருமை (orumai, 'one birth') is set against எழுமை (ezhumai, 'seven births'), a conventional expression for a long chain of future lives. The key word ஏமாப்பு (emaappu) means protection, security or support, so learning is pictured as a lasting safeguard that goes with the soul. Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah follow the traditional rebirth reading. Kalaignar reinterprets it more secularly as learning that protects seven generations of a family. The kural fits the chapter's larger claim that learning, unlike other goods, is not used up or lost. Similar ideas appear in the Gita's teaching that a yogi's progress carries over into the next life and in Plato's theory that learning is recollection from earlier existence.

tamil:
தாமின் புறுவது உலகின் புறக்கண்டு
காமுறுவர் கற்றறிந் தார்.
transliteration:
Thaaminburuvadhu ulaginburak kandu
Kaamuruvar katrarindhaar.
current_meaning: When learned people see that the learning that brings them joy also brings joy to the whole world, they love learning even more.
elementary: When you discover a great story and tell your friends, they love it too, and that makes you want to find even more stories. Learning works like that. Sharing it makes everyone happy, so you want to learn more.
university: The kural describes a self-reinforcing cycle of joy. The learned find pleasure (இன்புறுவது) in their own knowledge, then see that the same knowledge brings pleasure to the world (உலகு இன்புற). That discovery makes them desire (காமுறுவர்) learning all the more. Valluvar's use of kaamam, a word more often tied to love and desire, is striking: learning becomes a passion. The kural suggests that the highest motive for study is neither prestige nor profit but shared delight, which makes knowledge a social good. The idea is echoed in Seneca's statement that he learns only in order to teach, and in the Mishnah and hadith traditions that praise those who learn in order to share.
